name: Abaloparatide
evidence: FDA Approved for osteoporosis. 'Black box' warning for osteosarcoma removed in 2021.
summary: Synthetic analog of parathyroid hormone-related protein, approved (Tymlos) for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and high-risk men. Builds bone by boosting formation, raising bone density and lowering vertebral and non-vertebral fracture risk.
mechanism: Selectively activates the PTH1 receptor, favoring RG over R0 signaling for an anabolic bias with less resorption. Promotes osteoblast differentiation and survival, raising cortical bone density and strength while shaping calcium handling.
safety: Can cause hypercalcemia, dizziness, and palpitations. Rodent-based osteosarcoma concern initially triggered a boxed warning, later removed or downgraded.

name: Adipotide
evidence: Peptidomimetic targeting prohibitin in white adipose tissue vasculature to induce apoptosis. Designed for rapid weight loss.
primaryUse: Targeted fat tissue reduction through vascular targeting
summary: Synthetic peptide (FTPP) built from a targeting domain and a pro-apoptotic domain, designed to destroy blood vessels feeding white fat. Shown in obese rhesus monkeys to cut body fat and improve insulin sensitivity; no approved use, human testing limited.
mechanism: The targeting segment binds prohibitin-1 on adipose-tissue endothelial cells; the attached pro-apoptotic segment collapses mitochondrial membrane potential in those cells, triggering apoptosis via MAPK-linked pathways and cutting local blood flow to fat.
safety: Renal toxicity risk is high; human trials stopped after proximal tubule damage and declining kidney function. Not considered safe for people.

name: Afamelanotide
evidence: FDA approved (Scenesse) for EPP. Implant delivery.
primaryUse: Treatment of erythropoietic protoporphyria and photosensitivity disorders
summary: Synthetic α-MSH analog approved (Scenesse) for erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare light-sensitivity disorder. Boosts eumelanin production to extend pain-free sun exposure.
mechanism: Agonizes melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes, raising cAMP and driving MITF-linked tyrosinase activity toward eumelanin over pheomelanin. Also curbs NF-κB-driven inflammation and supports DNA-repair and antioxidant responses.
safety: Implant-site reactions are common, along with nausea, headache, and darkened skin. Anaphylaxis is rare.

name: AHK-Cu (Copper Peptide)
evidence: Promotes hair follicle elongation and proliferation of dermal papilla cells. Used as a gentler alternative to Minoxidil.
summary: Synthetic copper-binding tripeptide (Ala-His-Lys) modeled on GHK-Cu, built for better stability and skin penetration. Studied for collagen stimulation, wound healing, and skin remodeling; mainly used in cosmetic products, not clinically approved.
mechanism: Delivers copper into cells, activating lysyl oxidase and prolyl hydroxylase to build collagen and elastin, while balancing MMP and TIMP activity for matrix remodeling. Also spurs VEGF-driven vessel growth and fibroblast/keratinocyte migration.
safety: Well tolerated with low toxicity; occasional mild local irritation or redness. Absorption profile resembles GHK-Cu.

name: AICAR (Acadesine)
evidence: No recent significant human clinical safety data (2020-2025). Older trials showed uric acid increase.
primaryUse: Metabolic enhancement and exercise performance improvement
summary: AMP-mimicking compound (also called Acadesine) that activates AMPK, a cellular energy-sensing enzyme. Used in research on metabolism, endurance, and glucose handling; sometimes called ‘exercise in a pill,’ but has no approved medical use.
mechanism: Converts intracellularly to ZMP, which binds AMPK’s γ subunit to activate it, boosting muscle glucose uptake via GLUT4 and fat burning via ACC inhibition, plus mitochondrial growth through PGC-1α.
safety: Not FDA approved. High doses may risk the kidneys, and it is banned by USADA as a doping agent.

name: AOD9604 (hGH Fragment 176-191)
evidence: Investigational for obesity and tissue repair. Clinical evidence is limited compared to approved metabolic drugs. No FDA approval.
primaryUse: Fat metabolism regulation and weight management
summary: Fragment of human growth hormone (amino acids 176–191) engineered in the 1990s to isolate hGH’s fat-burning action from its growth effects. Studied for fat loss and possibly joint/tissue repair; remains investigational with no approval.
mechanism: Mimics hGH’s lipid effects via β3-adrenergic receptor activation in fat tissue, raising cAMP/PKA signaling and hormone-sensitive lipase activity to break down triglycerides, without affecting glucose or IGF-1.
safety: Generally well tolerated; mild injection-site reactions, headache, nausea reported. Unlike hGH it doesn’t raise IGF-1 or cause insulin resistance, but WADA prohibits it.

name: ARA-290 (Cibinetide)
approval: Phase 2 Clinical Trial (Completed). Granted orphan drug designation for sarcoidosis and pancreatic islet transplantation.
evidence: Phase 2 clinical trial for Diabetic Macular Edema completed. Extensive preclinical research shows neuroprotection, organ protection (e.g., against cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity, 2022), and potential to ameliorate frailty in mouse models.
primaryUse: Treatment of small fiber neuropathy and nerve protection
summary: 11-amino-acid peptide derived from erythropoietin that activates the innate repair receptor for tissue protection without stimulating red blood cell production. Holds FDA orphan status for sarcoidosis and islet-transplant survival; completed a Phase 2 trial in diabetic macular edema, with preclinical work in neuropathy, Alzheimer’s, and drug-induced kidney injury.
mechanism: Binds the innate repair receptor (a CD131/EPOR-beta complex), triggering JAK2/STAT3 and PI3K/Akt signaling that protects nerve tissue from apoptosis, curbs inflammation, and supports nerve regeneration and pain reduction.
safety: Generally well tolerated in trials, with mild, transient side effects.

name: Argireline (Acetyl Hexapeptide-3 / Acetyl Hexapeptide-8)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
primaryUse: Reduction of expression wrinkles and fine lines
summary: Synthetic hexapeptide from Lipotec (2001), designed as a topical, non-injectable alternative to botulinum toxin. Mimics part of SNAP-25 to soften expression wrinkles; used widely in cosmetics, with effects reported milder than injectable neurotoxins.
mechanism: Competitively blocks SNAP-25 from joining the SNARE complex, reducing acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions and dampening the muscle contractions that form expression lines.
safety: Considered good; well tolerated in cosmetic use.

name: Atosiban
evidence: Oxytocin and vasopressin receptor antagonist used to delay preterm birth (24-33 weeks). Standard of care in many regions (EU).
primaryUse: Prevention of preterm labor in pregnancy
summary: Synthetic oxytocin-receptor antagonist from 1985, used to delay preterm labor by blocking oxytocin’s effect on the uterus. Delays birth by at least 48 hours, allowing time for corticosteroids to mature fetal lungs; a standard tocolytic in Europe but not FDA-approved in the US.
mechanism: Competitively blocks oxytocin (and to a lesser extent vasopressin V1a) receptors on uterine muscle, cutting calcium-driven contractions via reduced phospholipase C/IP3 signaling, and lowering inflammatory cytokines linked to labor onset.
safety: Favorable safety profile; nausea (~14%), headache, and injection-site reactions are the main effects, with lower cardiovascular risk than beta-mimetics and no observed fetal toxicity.

name: B7-33
evidence: Optimized H2 relaxin analogue. Anti-fibrotic and vasoprotective effects without the hemodynamic side effects of native relaxin.
summary: Synthetic single-chain peptide derived from H2 relaxin, engineered in 2016 for better stability while keeping relaxin’s cardiovascular benefits. Shows anti-fibrotic, vessel-protective effects in animal heart-failure and fibrosis models; still preclinical, no human trials yet.
mechanism: Selectively activates RXFP1 receptors, raising cAMP/NO signaling and eNOS-driven nitric oxide for vasodilation, while suppressing TGF-β/Smad2 and MMP activity to limit cardiac fibrosis and inflammation.
safety: Appears promising; unlike native relaxin it doesn’t trigger the cAMP pathway linked to fast heart rate and tumor growth, with minimal adverse effects in animals.

name: Belantamab mafodotin
approval: FDA Approved (2020, withdrew 2023, re-approved 2025 for combination therapy)
evidence: Combination therapy with bortezomib and dexamethasone showed improved outcomes (2025 approval)
summary: Antibody-drug conjugate targeting BCMA, first FDA-approved in 2020, withdrawn in 2023, then re-approved in October 2025 with bortezomib and dexamethasone for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma. Delivers a cytotoxic payload directly to myeloma cells.
mechanism: An afucosylated IgG1 antibody binds BCMA on myeloma cells and, once internalized and cleaved, releases the microtubule inhibitor MMAF, arresting the cell cycle and driving apoptosis.
safety: Carries a boxed warning for eye toxicity, including corneal changes and vision loss; available only through a restricted REMS program.
boxedWarning: Risk of ocular toxicity including corneal epithelium changes. REMS program required

name: BPC-157
legal: Unapproved New Drug (FDA Category 2 bulk drug substance). Prohibited by WADA.
approval: Not FDA Approved for human or animal use.
evidence: Limited Human Studies
sideEffects: Injection site reactions (pain, swelling, infection, allergic reactions)
summary: Synthetic peptide based on a protective gastric-juice protein, studied in animals for angiogenesis, cellular repair, and cytoprotective/anti-inflammatory effects on tendons, ligaments, gut, and brain. Not FDA-approved, classified as an unapproved drug, and banned by WADA; human evidence is very limited.
mechanism: Raises VEGF-driven blood vessel formation and growth-hormone receptor expression, boosts collagen formation, and activates the FAK-paxillin pathway for cell migration; also promotes nitric oxide release and mucosal defense in the gut.
safety: Appears safe in animals with no reported toxicity, but human safety data from controlled trials is lacking; theoretical concern about supporting tumor growth via VEGFR2 activation.

name: Brilacidin (PMX-30063)
evidence: Host defense protein (Defensin) mimetic. Investigational for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), Oral Mucositis, and viral infections.
primaryUse: Treatment of bacterial infections and inflammation
summary: Synthetic defensin-mimetic antibiotic from Innovation Pharmaceuticals (2009), designed to imitate the body’s natural host-defense peptides. Active against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, including resistant strains; in clinical development for skin infections, oral mucositis, and inflammatory bowel disease, with favorable Phase 2 results so far.
mechanism: Disrupts bacterial membranes through electrostatic binding to negatively charged phospholipids, causing depolarization and death, while also dampening inflammation via toll-like receptor modulation and reduced NF-κB, TNF-α, and IL-1β activity.
safety: Generally well tolerated in trials; mild, transient tingling/numbness with IV dosing, no hemolysis observed, and serious adverse events are rare.

name: Bronchogen (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu)
evidence: Synthetic tetrapeptide bioregulator. Investigated for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma adjunct therapy.
primaryUse: Respiratory immune system support and regulation
summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu) from Russian “peptide bioregulator” research, intended to support respiratory function and studied there for bronchitis and asthma. Lacks recent international clinical research and is not FDA/EMA approved; sold online as a supplement or research chemical.
mechanism: Thought to act on immune cells in bronchial tissue via JAK/STAT signaling, balancing cytokine output, boosting macrophage activity while curbing IL-6 and TNF-α, and supporting T-cell regulation and epithelial barrier integrity.
safety: Marketed as side-effect-free, but rigorous human trial data is absent; preclinical tolerability appears good.

name: Cagrilintide
evidence: Phase 3 trials (REDEFINE). Often studied with semaglutide (CagriSema).
primaryUse: Treatment of obesity and metabolic disorders
summary: Long-acting amylin analog in Phase 3 development for weight management, mimicking amylin’s satiety and gastric-slowing effects. Being developed alone and combined with semaglutide (CagriSema) for greater weight loss than either drug alone.
mechanism: Agonizes calcitonin receptors, activating cAMP/PKA signaling in hypothalamic neurons to boost satiety, while slowing gastric emptying and suppressing after-meal glucagon; structural modifications extend its half-life for infrequent dosing.
safety: Nausea and vomiting are common; no increased pancreatitis signal so far, and cardiovascular profile appears favorable.

name: Calcitonin (Salmon)
approval: FDA Approved (Miacalcin injection: 1986; Fortical nasal spray: 2005) + EMA Approved
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
primaryUse: Treatment of osteoporosis and bone disorders
summary: Synthetic peptide hormone mimicking human calcitonin, approved since the 1980s–2000s (Miacalcin, Fortical) for postmenopausal osteoporosis, Paget’s disease, and hypercalcemia by curbing osteoclast activity and calcium reabsorption. Long-term use carries a cancer-risk signal, so the FDA recommends it only when other options aren’t suitable.
mechanism: Binds calcitonin receptors on osteoclasts, raising cAMP to reduce osteoclast movement, ruffled-border formation, and enzyme secretion, cutting bone resorption; also lowers renal and intestinal calcium reabsorption and has CNS-mediated analgesic effects.
safety: Long-term use is linked to increased cancer risk. Common effects include nausea, flushing, injection reactions, rhinitis, and headache; rare risks include severe allergy and low calcium.
boxedWarning: Increased risk of certain cancers with long-term use.

name: Cardiogen (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg)
evidence: Limited to Russian preclinical studies; no human clinical trials have been conducted.
summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) from Russian bioregulator research, intended to support cardiovascular tissue. Studied there without recent international clinical data; not FDA/EMA approved and sold as a research chemical.
mechanism: Believed to modulate gene expression in heart cells, encouraging cardiomyocyte growth while limiting fibroblast activity and scarring, boosting structural protein production, and possibly reducing apoptosis via lowered p53 expression.
safety: Data is limited; animal studies suggest good tolerability, but no human trials exist, so human safety is unknown.

name: Carfilzomib
evidence: FDA approved (Kyprolis). Ongoing trials for new combinations.
primaryUse: Treatment of relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma
summary: Selective proteasome inhibitor approved (Kyprolis) for multiple myeloma, typically after prior therapies. Blocks protein breakdown in cancer cells, causing toxic protein buildup and cell death.
mechanism: Irreversibly binds the β5 subunit of the 20S proteasome/immunoproteasome’s catalytic threonine, blocking chymotrypsin-like activity; this piles up ubiquitinated proteins, triggering ER stress, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis, especially in high-protein-turnover myeloma cells.
safety: Carries serious cardiovascular risks (heart failure, ischemia), kidney toxicity, and blood-cell toxicity (low platelets); needs close monitoring.

name: Cartalax (Ala-Glu-Asp)
evidence: Synthetic tripeptide bioregulator targeting cartilage and connective tissue. Used for joint health and osteoarthritis.
primaryUse: Joint cartilage protection and regeneration support
summary: Synthetic tripeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp) from the early 2000s, studied for cartilage protection and joint health. Preclinical work suggests it may regulate cartilage-degrading enzymes and support proteoglycan/collagen production; remains an unapproved research peptide with limited human data.
mechanism: Interacts with chondrocyte receptors to boost proteoglycan and type II collagen synthesis, inhibits cartilage-degrading MMPs while raising TIMPs, reduces IL-1β/TNF-α inflammation, and supports chondrocyte survival via PI3K/Akt signaling.
safety: Generally reported well tolerated where used, with possible mild allergic reaction or injection-site irritation; long-term human safety data is scarce.

name: Cerebrolysin
approval: Approved in many countries (e.g., Russia, China, Germany, Austria); Not FDA Approved in the USA.
evidence: Numerous clinical trials. A 2023 Cochrane review found little to no benefit in preventing death from acute ischemic stroke, while a 2024 assessment suggested benefits in neurological recovery. The overall strength of evidence is still debated.
summary: Neuropeptide mixture from purified porcine brain proteins, used clinically in 50+ countries for acute ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and dementia, though not FDA-approved. Recent systematic reviews (2023–2024) give mixed results on stroke efficacy, keeping its evidence base debated.
mechanism: Contains fragments resembling BDNF, GDNF, NGF, and CNTF; crosses the blood-brain barrier to activate BDNF/TrkB and PI3K/Akt signaling for neuron survival and plasticity, supports synaptic remodeling via MAPK/ERK, and curbs inflammation and glutamate-driven excitotoxicity.
safety: Generally has a strong safety record, though some data suggest higher doses in acute stroke may raise non-fatal serious adverse events.

name: Chonluten (Glu-Asp-Arg)
evidence: Tripeptide bioregulator with affinity for lung and gastrointestinal tissues. Studied for anti-inflammatory and gene regulation effects.
primaryUse: Cartilage and joint tissue regeneration support
summary: Synthetic tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) from 1990s research into joint and cartilage support. Animal studies suggest possible joint-health benefits through anti-inflammatory and repair-promoting activity; remains an unapproved research peptide with limited human study.
mechanism: Acts on chondrocyte receptors to boost proteoglycan and type II collagen synthesis, suppresses IL-1β/TNF-α via reduced NF-κB signaling, supports chondrocyte survival through PI3K/Akt, and lowers cartilage-degrading MMP expression.
safety: Reported to have minimal side effects in bioregulator research, but lacks rigorous human safety data; long-term effects are unknown.

name: CJC-1295 (with and without DAC)
approval: Not FDA Approved; Prohibited by WADA. Re-evaluated by FDA in 2024 for potential compounding.
evidence: No active or recent clinical trials. Early-phase studies were conducted prior to 2020 but did not lead to clinical approval.
summary: Long-acting synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone, shown in early studies to raise GH and IGF-1 levels. Not FDA-approved for any use, with no major 2020–2025 trials; banned by WADA and sold as a research chemical, though a 2024 FDA status review opened it to further compounding evaluation without approving it.
mechanism: Binds GHRH receptors on the pituitary to trigger GH release via cAMP signaling. The DAC version attaches to serum albumin, extending its half-life from about 30 minutes to 6–8 days for sustained GH/IGF-1 elevation; the non-DAC form (Mod GRF 1-29) acts more briefly.
safety: Long-term human safety is unknown. The FDA has flagged cardiac event risk, plus concerns tied to elevated GH/IGF-1, including insulin resistance.

name: Copper-64 Dotatate
evidence: 90.9% sensitivity, 96.6% specificity for detecting NETs
indication: PET imaging of somatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors
summary: FDA-approved (2020) radiopharmaceutical for PET imaging of somatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors. Its longer half-life versus gallium-68 agents allows sharper imaging and simpler daily production.
mechanism: Binds preferentially to somatostatin receptor type 2, overexpressed on neuroendocrine tumor cells, and its copper-64 positron emission allows PET visualization of receptor-bearing tumors.
safety: Excellent safety record; no serious adverse events in trials, with minor reactions in under 2% of cases.

name: Cortagen (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro)
evidence: Limited to preclinical studies. No significant human clinical trials.
summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro), one of the Russian “Khavinson peptides,” developed for cognitive support and neuroprotection. Suggested in research to preserve cognition under stress and aid memory through effects on neurotransmitters and neuroplasticity; not FDA-approved, with limited human study.
mechanism: Thought to mimic ACTH fragments and modulate neural gene expression via cAMP/PKA signaling and NMDA receptor activity, while promoting BDNF and reducing inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress in neural tissue.
safety: Generally well tolerated in animal studies; human safety data is very limited.

name: Cosyntropin (Tetracosactide)
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
primaryUse: Diagnostic testing of adrenal gland function
summary: Synthetic ACTH analog (first 24 amino acids) from the 1960s, used as the gold-standard diagnostic test for adrenal function under brand names Synacthen and Cortrosyn. Some research also explores therapeutic use in certain autoimmune conditions.
mechanism: Binds melanocortin-2 receptors on adrenal cortex cells, raising cAMP and PKA activity that mobilizes cholesterol via StAR protein regulation, driving cortisol and other adrenal steroid synthesis.
safety: Good.

name: CT-388
evidence: Phase 1/2 trials ongoing. Dual GLP-1/GIP agonist.
primaryUse: Skin regeneration and collagen synthesis enhancement
summary: Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist in Phase 2 development by Roche/Carmot Therapeutics for obesity and type 2 diabetes. Early data suggest strong weight loss and glucose control, similar to other dual agonists like tirzepatide.
safety: Consistent with other incretin drugs; mainly GI effects, with no unexpected safety signals in early trials.

name: Cyclosporine (Neoral, Sandimmune, Gengraf)
evidence: FDA-approved Calcineurin inhibitor. Standard for transplant rejection prophylaxis, severe psoriasis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Ophthalmic drops for dry eye.
summary: Cyclic polypeptide immunosuppressant approved to prevent organ-transplant rejection and treat severe autoimmune diseases like psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis by blocking calcineurin-driven T-cell activation. Effective for quick disease control but usually limited to 1–2 year courses given nephrotoxicity and hypertension risks; recent work (2020–2025) focuses on rescue-therapy use, side-effect management, and topical delivery to cut systemic exposure.
mechanism: Forms a complex with cyclophilin that inhibits calcineurin, blocking NFAT activation and nuclear entry, which suppresses IL-2 and other cytokine genes needed for T-cell proliferation; also affects B-cells, dendritic cells, P-glycoprotein expression, and calcium handling.
safety: Systemic use risks kidney and liver damage, high blood pressure, and higher infection/cancer risk (skin cancer, lymphoma); ophthalmic use is mostly safe, causing mild burning or stinging.

name: Dapiglutide (ZP7570)
evidence: Long-acting GLP-1/GLP-2 dual agonist. Investigational for obesity and improving intestinal barrier function.
primaryUse: Treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes
summary: Investigational dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist peptide (ZP7570) from the early 2020s, designed for enhanced metabolic benefit over single-receptor incretins. In early clinical development for type 2 diabetes and obesity, with once-weekly dosing under study; preclinical data show reduced glucose and body weight in animals.
mechanism: Activates both GLP-1 and GIP receptors, raising cAMP/PKA signaling to boost glucose-dependent insulin release, cut glucagon secretion, and slow gastric emptying; structural changes extend half-life and resist DPP-4 breakdown.
safety: Mostly mild-to-moderate nausea and vomiting, with some mild injection-site reactions; anti-drug antibodies appeared in about 14% of participants, with no serious drug-related events reported early on.

name: Daptomycin (Cubicin)
evidence: FDA-approved cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic (Cubicin). First-line alternative for resistant Gram-positive infections (MRSA, VRE).
primaryUse: Treatment of serious gram-positive bacterial infections
summary: Cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic from Streptomyces roseosporus (1980s), approved by the FDA and EMA for complicated skin infections and bacteremia, including MRSA and right-sided endocarditis. Kills bacteria in both growing and stationary phases via a distinctive membrane-disrupting mechanism that resists cross-resistance.
mechanism: Calcium-dependently inserts into bacterial membranes, binding phosphatidylglycerol to trigger depolarization and potassium efflux; pore/channel formation causes cellular leakage and death without targeting cell-wall or protein synthesis.
safety: Muscle toxicity (myopathy, rhabdomyolysis) is the main risk, requiring weekly CPK checks; rare eosinophilic pneumonia and peripheral neuropathy with long-term use are also reported.

name: Dasiglucagon
evidence: FDA Approved (Zegalogue) for severe hypoglycemia.
primaryUse: Treatment of severe hypoglycemia in diabetes patients
summary: Stable, soluble glucagon analog approved (Zegalogue) for severe hypoglycemia in adults and children with diabetes. Comes as a ready-to-use liquid, unlike traditional glucagon that needs reconstituting.
mechanism: Agonizes the glucagon receptor on liver cells, raising cAMP to activate glycogen phosphorylase and inhibit glycogen synthase, releasing stored glucose, while also boosting gluconeogenesis enzymes like PEPCK.
safety: Nausea, vomiting, and headache are common; generally considered safe for emergency rescue use.

name: DaxibotulinumtoxinA
evidence: SAKURA trials: median 168-day (24-week) duration maintaining 'none' or 'mild' severity
summary: 150-kDa botulinum toxin type A formulated with a stabilizing peptide (RTP004) that removes human serum albumin and allows room-temperature storage. FDA-approved in 2022 for moderate-to-severe glabellar lines, with effects lasting a median of six months, up to nine in some patients.
mechanism: Cleaves the SNAP25 protein needed for acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, dose-dependently reducing muscle contraction.
safety: Similar safety profile to other botulinum toxin products.

name: Decapeptide-12 (Lumixyl)
evidence: Demonstrated efficacy for hyperpigmentation and vitiligo. Particularly noted for safety in ethnic skin types where other agents may be cytotoxic.
summary: Synthetic oligopeptide developed at Stanford (2009) as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone for hyperpigmentation. Competitively inhibits tyrosinase to cut melanin production without harming melanocytes; used in cosmetic products for melasma, age spots, and post-inflammatory marks, with in vitro melanin reduction up to 40%.
mechanism: Binds the active site of tyrosinase, blocking the conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and dopaquinone, and lowers inflammatory cytokines in keratinocytes without destroying melanocytes.
safety: Well tolerated topically; mild dryness, itching, irritation, or transient burning can occur, with no notable systemic effects.

name: Degarelix
evidence: FDA approved for advanced prostate cancer. Comparative studies vs GnRH agonists.
summary: GnRH receptor antagonist approved (Firmagon) for advanced prostate cancer. Rapidly lowers testosterone without the initial surge seen with GnRH agonists, giving immediate hormonal control.
mechanism: Competitively blocks pituitary GnRH receptors, cutting LH and FSH release and suppressing testosterone within 24–48 hours, without the flare caused by agonist drugs.
safety: Injection-site pain and redness are very common; hot flashes, weight gain, and liver enzyme rises can occur, with a better cardiovascular profile than GnRH agonists.

name: Desmopressin
evidence: FDA-approved synthetic vasopressin analog (DDAVP). Treats central diabetes insipidus, primary nocturnal enuresis, and von Willebrand disease (Type 1).
primaryUse: Treatment of diabetes insipidus and fluid regulation
summary: Synthetic vasopressin analog from 1967, engineered for stronger antidiuretic effect with less vasopressor activity. Used worldwide as first-line treatment for central diabetes insipidus and nocturnal enuresis, and in mild hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease.
mechanism: Selectively activates kidney V2 receptors, raising cAMP to insert aquaporin-2 channels into collecting-duct cells, concentrating urine; also releases von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII, aiding clotting.
safety: Main risk is hyponatremia (water intoxication), which can cause seizures or coma; also headache, nausea, flushing; avoid in heart failure, kidney impairment, or uncontrolled hypertension.

name: Difelikefalin
evidence: KALM-1 and KALM-2 Phase 3 trials demonstrated significant pruritus reduction vs placebo
summary: Selective kappa opioid receptor agonist approved in 2021 as the first treatment for moderate-to-severe itching in adult hemodialysis patients with chronic kidney disease. Has over 10,000-fold greater affinity for kappa than mu opioid receptors, giving minimal brain effects.
mechanism: Activates kappa opioid receptors on peripheral sensory nerves and immune cells to dampen itch signaling, without central nervous system or mu-receptor involvement.
safety: Favorable profile; no respiratory depression, sedation, or euphoria, and low addiction potential.

name: Dihexa
evidence: Angiotensin IV analog and HGF/c-Met activator. Promotes synaptogenesis and neurogenesis. Investigated for neurodegenerative diseases.
summary: Synthetic peptide from Washington State University (2012), built from a modified angiotensin IV to improve stability and brain penetration. Acts as an HGF mimetic promoting nerve growth and connections; studied preclinically for cognitive decline and neurodegeneration, but remains unapproved with limited human data.
mechanism: Agonizes the c-Met receptor, activating MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling that drives neurogenesis, synapse formation, and dendritic spine growth, while raising BDNF expression.
safety: Human safety is unknown; theoretical cancer risk from activating the c-Met oncogenic pathway, and possible overstimulation, anxiety, or irritability.

name: Donanemab
evidence: Slowed decline by 35% over 18 months. Reduced amyloid plaques by 84% vs baseline
summary: Humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody approved in July 2024 for early Alzheimer’s disease with confirmed amyloid buildup. Targets a toxic form of amyloid beta in plaques; trials showed 35% slower decline over 18 months and an 84% drop in plaque levels, and treatment can stop once amyloid is sufficiently cleared.
mechanism: Binds insoluble, N-truncated pyroglutamate amyloid-beta in brain plaques, clearing them from the brain.
safety: Boxed warning for ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding from amyloid clearance); three trial deaths were linked to ARIA.
boxedWarning: ARIA - risk of brain swelling and bleeding. MRI monitoring required

name: DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide)
evidence: Neuropeptide with sleep-promoting and stress-reducing properties. Clinical efficacy remains inconsistent.
summary: Naturally occurring nonapeptide discovered in 1977 in rabbit brain tissue during sleep research. Studied for effects on sleep regulation, stress reduction, and pain modulation via GABA and serotonin pathways; remains an unapproved research compound with limited clinical evidence.
mechanism: Enhances GABA receptor activity and adenosine signaling in sleep-regulating brain regions, dampens the HPA stress axis to lower cortisol, and interacts with the suprachiasmatic nucleus to shape circadian and delta-wave sleep patterns.
safety: Long-term human safety unknown; grogginess and headache reported anecdotally, with an FDA warning about serious immune reactions from compounded versions and possible interaction with other sedatives.

name: Dulaglutide (Trulicity)
evidence: FDA-approved once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist. Significantly reduces HbA1c and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in Type 2 Diabetes.
summary: Long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist (Trulicity), approved in 2014, pairing a modified GLP-1 sequence with an IgG4 Fc fragment for once-weekly dosing. Improves blood sugar, promotes weight loss, and reduces cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes.
mechanism: Activates GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells via cAMP/PKA and PI3K/Akt signaling, boosting glucose-dependent insulin release, cutting glucagon, and slowing gastric emptying; the Fc fragment extends its half-life to about five days, and central GLP-1 activation raises satiety.
safety: Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors (from animal data); GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, vomiting) are common, with risks of pancreatitis, kidney injury, and gallbladder disease.

name: Ecnoglutide (XW003)
evidence: Phase 3 trials ongoing (SLIMMER, T2DM). Shown superiority to placebo and comparable safety to dulaglutide.
primaryUse: Treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity
summary: Long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist (XW003) from Sciwind Biosciences, optimized for potency and manufacturing cost. Trials show meaningful weight loss and HbA1c reduction in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
mechanism: Selectively binds GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells, raising cAMP for glucose-dependent insulin release; structural changes resist DPP-4 breakdown for a longer half-life, while hypothalamic receptor activation curbs appetite and slows gastric emptying.
safety: Consistent with other GLP-1 drugs; GI effects (nausea, diarrhea) are most common, with low trial discontinuation rates.

name: Efinopegdutide (HM15211 / MK-6024)
evidence: Phase 2 trials ongoing for NASH/MASLD. Granted FDA Fast Track Designation.
primaryUse: Treatment of NASH and metabolic liver diseases
summary: Dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist (HM15211/MK-6024) from Hanmi, licensed to Merck, under investigation for MASH and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, with FDA Fast Track status for NASH.
safety: Generally well tolerated; adverse effects are mostly gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting), similar to other GLP-1 drugs.

name: Elsiglutide
approval: Investigational - Phase 2B completed (did not meet primary endpoint)
evidence: Phase 2B: diarrhea rates 3-10% but not statistically significant. Preclinical: protective effects confirmed
sideEffects: Well tolerated - GI effects typical for class
summary: GLP-2 analog studied for preventing chemotherapy-induced diarrhea by boosting intestinal lining growth. A Phase 2B trial in colorectal cancer patients showed lower diarrhea rates than placebo, but the difference wasn’t statistically significant; preclinical work showed protection against chemotherapy-related mucositis and diarrhea.
mechanism: Activates GLP-2 pathways to increase intestinal epithelial cell proliferation and reduce cell death, replacing cells damaged by chemotherapy.
safety: Generally well tolerated in trials.

name: Enfuvirtide
evidence: FDA-approved HIV fusion inhibitor (Fuzeon). Used in combination therapy for treatment-experienced patients.
primaryUse: HIV entry inhibitor for drug-resistant infections
summary: Synthetic 36-amino-acid peptide from the 1990s, the first HIV fusion inhibitor and first peptide-based antiretroviral, approved by the FDA in 2003. Mimics part of HIV’s gp41 protein to block viral entry into T-cells; used in salvage therapy for treatment-experienced, multi-drug-resistant HIV patients.
mechanism: Binds the HR1 region of HIV’s gp41 envelope protein, preventing the six-helix bundle formation needed for virus-cell membrane fusion, blocking entry before infection; active against both CCR5- and CXCR4-tropic strains.
safety: Injection-site reactions are nearly universal (about 98%) and can be painful; increased bacterial pneumonia risk and rare but serious hypersensitivity reactions.

name: Epitalon (Epithalon)
evidence: Synthetic tetrapeptide telomerase activator. Investigated for life extension, anti-aging, and sleep regulation (pineal gland modulation).
primaryUse: Circadian rhythm regulation and anti-aging effects
summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) developed by Vladimir Khavinson’s institute in the 1980s to mimic pineal peptide epithalamin. Studied in Russia for effects on melatonin release, circadian rhythm, and cellular aging via telomerase activity; not approved in Western markets, with no rigorous Western clinical trials.
mechanism: Boosts telomerase activity and modulates chromatin and gene expression in the pineal gland, stimulating serotonin N-acetyltransferase to raise melatonin; also activates MAPK/ERK for neuroprotection and raises antioxidant enzyme activity.
safety: Long-term human safety not established; theoretical cancer-promotion risk from telomerase activation, though anecdotally well tolerated with mild effects like vivid dreams.

name: Exenatide (Byetta, Bydureon)
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
primaryUse: Treatment of type 2 diabetes and weight management
summary: Synthetic GLP-1 receptor agonist marketed as twice-daily Byetta (approved 2005) and once-weekly extended-release Bydureon (approved 2012). Mimics GLP-1 to boost insulin, suppress glucagon, slow digestion, and reduce appetite in type 2 diabetes, often with modest weight loss.
mechanism: Shares 53% sequence identity with human GLP-1 and activates GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells via cAMP/PKA and PI3K/Akt signaling; resists DPP-4 breakdown for a longer half-life, slows gastric emptying via vagal signaling, and supports beta-cell survival through CREB activation.
safety: Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors; common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache; risks include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia with other diabetes drugs, kidney injury, and gallbladder disease.
boxedWarning: Risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) with Bydureon BCise. Contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

name: FGL (Fibroblast Growth Loop peptide - Plannexin, FGLs, FGLL)
evidence: Neural Cell Adhesion Molecule (NCAM) mimetic. Promotes neurite outgrowth and synaptic plasticity. Investigational for Alzheimer's/TBI.
primaryUse: Enhancement of cognitive function and neural plasticity
summary: Synthetic peptide mimic of neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM), developed in the early 2000s for cognitive enhancement and neuroprotection. Activates FGF receptor signaling to boost synaptic plasticity and BDNF; shown in animals to aid neurogenesis, learning, and memory, but remains research-only with limited human data.
mechanism: Binds FGFR1, triggering receptor dimerization and MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling that raises BDNF via CREB-driven gene expression, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and strengthens synaptic transmission, long-term potentiation, and dendritic spine formation.
safety: Appears well tolerated in early studies; intranasal use caused only minor local irritation, with no systemic toxicity in animals.

name: Flotufolastat F-18
evidence: LIGHTHOUSE and SPOTLIGHT Phase 3 trials: high correct detection rate, clinically meaningful upstaging, effective at low PSA levels
indication: PET imaging of PSMA-positive prostate cancer lesions
summary: FDA-approved (May 2023) radiohybrid PSMA-targeted PET imaging agent for prostate cancer, with high PSMA binding affinity and unusually low bladder activity. Improves visualization of pelvic lesions, especially after prostatectomy or with recurrence, and works even at low PSA levels.
mechanism: Binds PSMA on prostate cancer cells and is taken up into them; its fluorine-18 label emits positrons for PET imaging.
safety: Well tolerated, typical for PET radiopharmaceuticals.

name: Follistatin (FS-315, FS-344)
evidence: Myostatin inhibitor promoting muscle hypertrophy. Investigational gene therapy for Becker Muscular Dystrophy. Peptide use is largely in the 'biohacking' community.
primaryUse: Muscle growth enhancement and muscle wasting treatment
summary: Naturally occurring protein first identified in 1987 as an inhibitor of follicle-stimulating hormone; FS-315 and FS-344 are studied variants for muscle growth and repair. Works by blocking myostatin and related TGF-β family signals; still in the research phase, with synthetic versions unapproved for medical use.
mechanism: Neutralizes myostatin and activin, removing their brake on muscle growth and triggering satellite-cell activation and myoblast proliferation via IGF-1/PI3K/Akt and mTOR signaling; also affects bone metabolism through BMP signaling and lowers inflammatory cytokines.
safety: Peptide safety data is mostly anecdotal (muscle soreness, tendon weakness); gene-therapy trials show good safety, but there’s theoretical concern over hormone disruption and mixed cancer-growth effects.

name: FOXO4-DRI (Proxofim)
evidence: Senolytic peptide designed to selectively clear senescent ('zombie') cells by disrupting FOXO4-p53 interaction. Investigational for anti-aging and frailty.
summary: Synthetic D-retro-inverso peptide (Proxofim) developed at Erasmus University Medical Center (2017) to selectively kill senescent (“zombie”) cells by disrupting FOXO4-p53 binding. Shown in mice to reduce age-related decline and support tissue function, especially in the brain; remains research-only with no human trials.
mechanism: Blocks the FOXO4-p53 interaction that normally protects senescent cells from death, causing p53 to move to mitochondria and trigger apoptosis selectively in senescent cells; crosses the blood-brain barrier to target senescent neural tissue.
safety: Human safety largely unestablished; theoretical risks include off-target apoptosis, immune activation, and metabolic disturbance, though animal models show good tolerability.

name: Gadopiclenol
evidence: PICTURE trial: non-inferior to gadobutrol at half the gadolinium dose
indication: MRI contrast agent for CNS and body imaging
sideEffects: Typical for gadolinium contrast agents - minimal
summary: Macrocyclic gadolinium-based MRI contrast agent approved in September 2022, engineered with a hydration number of 2 for two-to-three times greater relaxivity than standard agents. Allows use at half the usual dose while maintaining diagnostic quality, cutting gadolinium exposure.
mechanism: Its macrocyclic structure lets gadolinium interact with twice the water molecules of standard agents, boosting relaxivity and tissue signal enhancement at a lower dose.
safety: Well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to other macrocyclic gadolinium agents.

name: Gallium-68 PSMA-11
evidence: 91% confirmation rate of prostate cancer in patients with positive PET readings (960-patient trials)
indication: PET imaging of PSMA-positive prostate cancer lesions
sideEffects: Minimal - typical for radiopharmaceutical imaging agents
summary: First molecular-targeted PET imaging drug for PSMA-positive prostate cancer lesions, FDA-approved December 2020. Used in patients with suspected metastasis being considered for surgery or radiation, or suspected recurrence based on rising PSA.
mechanism: Binds PSMA on prostate cancer cells; its gallium-68 label emits positrons for PET visualization of PSMA-positive lesions.
safety: Well tolerated, with minimal adverse effects.

name: GHK Basic (Tripeptide-1)
evidence: Cosmetic clinical studies showing efficacy for skin aging.
summary: Copper-free version of the tripeptide GHK (Tripeptide-1), a signaling molecule known for boosting collagen production, wound healing, and skin anti-aging effects. Common ingredient in high-end skincare.
mechanism: Modulates matrix metalloproteinases and binds cell-surface receptors and copper to drive collagen and proteoglycan synthesis, fibroblast growth and migration, and release of VEGF, FGF, and NGF; also engages TGF-β/SMAD signaling and antioxidant defenses.
safety: Safe for topical use; irritation is rare.

name: GHK-Cu (Copper Peptide)
evidence: Extensively studied for skin remodeling, wound healing, and anti-aging. Promotes collagen synthesis and reduces inflammation.
summary: Copper-bound tripeptide first isolated from human plasma in 1973 during liver regeneration research. Promotes collagen synthesis, wound healing, hair follicle activity, and skin elasticity, with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects; widely used in cosmetics rather than as a medical treatment.
mechanism: Balances matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors to remodel collagen, elastin, and proteoglycans; drives fibroblast growth via TGF-β/SMAD signaling, recruits stem cells and growth factors (VEGF, FGF, NGF) to wounds, and lowers inflammatory cytokines while raising antioxidant activity.
safety: Very safe topically, with occasional mild irritation. Injectable/systemic use risks copper toxicity if unmonitored; avoid in Wilson’s disease or active cancer.

name: GHRP-2
evidence: Effective growth hormone secretagogue used clinically for diagnosing GH deficiency. Increases GH and IGF-1 levels reliably.
summary: Synthetic hexapeptide from the 1990s that mimics ghrelin to stimulate growth hormone release, with possible effects on body composition, sleep, and cellular repair; works synergistically with GHRH analogs. Remains an unapproved research chemical.
mechanism: Agonizes the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) in the pituitary, triggering calcium-driven growth hormone release via phospholipase C/IP3-DAG signaling, while also boosting hypothalamic GHRH and suppressing somatostatin; has mild effects on prolactin and ACTH too.
safety: Generally well tolerated; increased appetite, weight gain, elevated blood sugar, fluid retention, and joint pain can occur. Banned by WADA.

name: GHRP-6
evidence: Phase 1 trials in humans completed; mostly preclinical data available.
summary: Synthetic hexapeptide growth hormone secretagogue acting on the ghrelin receptor, researched for muscle mass, injury recovery, and body composition. Long history of research use but not FDA-approved.
mechanism: Binds the ghrelin/GHS receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, activating phospholipase C and calcium/protein kinase C signaling to boost GH release and pulse amplitude, while also raising ghrelin, appetite, IGF-1, prolactin, and cortisol somewhat.
safety: Generally well tolerated short-term; notably increases hunger, plus water retention, tingling, and fatigue.

name: Glatiramer Acetate
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
summary: Synthetic four-amino-acid protein mixture from 1960s research at the Weizmann Institute, designed to resemble myelin basic protein. A first-line, immune-modulating treatment for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (Copaxone, generic Glatopa), with over 20 years of safety and efficacy data reducing relapses and disability progression.
mechanism: Competes with myelin antigens for presentation to T cells, shifting the immune response from inflammatory Th1 toward anti-inflammatory Th2 cells and regulatory T cells, and pushes antigen-presenting cells toward an anti-inflammatory state while boosting neuroprotective BDNF.
safety: Excellent.

name: Glucagon
evidence: FDA Approved (Gvoke, Baqsimi). New stable formulations.
summary: Pancreatic peptide hormone that raises blood glucose, used as emergency treatment for severe hypoglycemia in diabetes. Newer stable liquid pens and intranasal powder formulations have replaced older kits requiring reconstitution.
mechanism: Binds the glucagon receptor on liver cells, raising cAMP and activating PKA to trigger glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis (via PEPCK and G6Pase), while suppressing glycolysis; also promotes fat oxidation and ketone production.
safety: Nausea and vomiting are very common; nasal forms may irritate; considered safe for emergency use.

name: Glutathione
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
sideEffects: Generally well-tolerated with minimal side effects at standard doses
summary: Naturally occurring tripeptide (glutamine, cysteine, glycine) first isolated in 1888, known as the body’s main antioxidant, supporting detoxification, immune function, and oxidative stress defense. Supplemental forms are used medically and in wellness settings; IV delivery gives the highest bioavailability since oral absorption is limited.
mechanism: Cycles between reduced and oxidized forms, with its cysteine thiol group neutralizing free radicals directly and serving as a cofactor for detox enzymes; supports T-cell function, dampens NF-κB-driven inflammation, and binds toxins/heavy metals for elimination.
safety: Excellent.

name: Gonadorelin (GnRH)
evidence: FDA Approved (Factrel). Used for fertility and precocious puberty.
summary: Synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), used diagnostically to test pituitary function and therapeutically — via pulsatile pump to induce ovulation, or via continuous agonist dosing to suppress sex hormones in conditions like endometriosis or prostate cancer.
mechanism: Binds pituitary GnRH receptors, activating Gq/11 signaling to raise calcium and protein kinase C, triggering LH and FSH release that drives gonadal steroid production; pulsatile dosing sustains reproductive function, while continuous dosing desensitizes receptors and suppresses it.
safety: Safe for diagnostic use; therapeutic use risks hot flashes, long-term bone density loss, and injection-site pain.

name: Goserelin (Zoladex)
evidence: FDA Approved (Zoladex). Extensive clinical use.
primaryUse: Treatment of hormone-sensitive cancers and gynecological conditions
summary: Synthetic GnRH agonist (Zoladex), FDA-approved for prostate cancer, breast cancer, endometriosis, and endometrial thinning. Overstimulates the pituitary until receptors downregulate, cutting testosterone or estrogen production.
mechanism: Initially boosts LH/FSH release via GnRH receptor activation (cAMP/PKA and IP3/calcium signaling), but continuous exposure desensitizes and internalizes the receptors, suppressing the pituitary-gonadal axis after an initial 1–2 week hormone flare.
safety: Hot flashes, sexual dysfunction, long-term bone density loss, injection-site injury, and an initial tumor flare.

name: Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH)
evidence: Endogenous hormone regulating GH secretion. Analogs (Tesamorelin) are FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. Diagnostic agent for GH deficiency.
primaryUse: Diagnostic agent for Growth Hormone Deficiency; its antagonists are under investigation for oncological applications.
summary: Hypothalamic peptide controlling growth hormone synthesis and release, mainly used diagnostically (GHRH-arginine test) for GH deficiency. Approved analogs like tesamorelin serve specific therapies, while recent research (2020–2025) focuses on GHRH receptor involvement in cancer growth, making GHRH antagonists an oncology target.
mechanism: Binds GHRH receptors on pituitary somatotrophs, raising cAMP/PKA signaling to open calcium channels and stimulate GH synthesis and secretion; works opposite somatostatin to create pulsatile GH release, modulated by IGF-1 feedback.
safety: Fluid retention, joint pain, and muscle aches are common; risks include hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and theoretical long-term diabetes or malignancy concerns.

name: Hexarelin
evidence: No FDA approval. Limited human studies (older).
summary: Synthetic hexapeptide and potent growth hormone secretagogue acting on the ghrelin receptor, promoting muscle growth and fat loss. Raises cortisol and prolactin more than other secretagogues and desensitizes the pituitary quickly, requiring cycling.
mechanism: Activates both the ghrelin receptor (GHSR-1a) in the pituitary, via calcium and protein kinase C signaling, and CD36 receptors in heart tissue, via MAPK/Akt pathways, supporting cardiomyocyte survival, mitochondrial function, and reduced oxidative stress/ischemia damage.
safety: Generally well tolerated short-term; theoretical cancer risk from growth factor stimulation, and raises cortisol/prolactin.

name: Humanin (and analogues like HNG)
evidence: Extensive preclinical research in animal and in-vitro models. No human clinical trials have been completed.
summary: 24-amino-acid mitochondria-derived peptide discovered in 2001, along with the more potent analog HNG. Shows neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects studied for Alzheimer’s, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic disorders; levels decline with age, and centenarians’ relatives show higher levels, hinting at a healthspan role. Not FDA-approved.
mechanism: Binds the formyl-peptide receptor FPRL1 and a CNTFR/WSX-1/gp130 receptor complex, activating JAK2/STAT3, ERK1/2, and PI3K/Akt signaling to block mitochondrial apoptosis (preventing Bax translocation and cytochrome c release); also improves insulin sensitivity via AMPK and blocks toxic amyloid-beta oligomer formation.
safety: Generally good, but long-term human safety unknown; some preclinical data suggest context-dependent effects on tumor growth.

name: HydrAMP-generated peptides
evidence: No human clinical trials for specific peptides found yet. Preclinical validation of AI-generated sequences.
summary: Not a single peptide but a generative AI (GAN) model that designs and optimizes antimicrobial peptides, improving stability and lowering toxicity while preserving activity against resistant bacteria.
mechanism: Generated peptides use patterned cationic/hydrophobic residues to electrostatically attach to and penetrate bacterial membranes, causing lysis, while also engaging toll-like receptor signaling to recruit neutrophils and macrophages and dampening excess inflammation via reduced NF-κB activity.
safety: Safety is optimized computationally; preclinical testing shows low toxicity for generated candidates.

name: Icatibant
evidence: FDA approved for Hereditary Angioedema (HAE). Real-world safety monitoring (IOS registry).
sideEffects: Temporary pain and swelling at injection site
summary: Selective bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist approved (Firazyr) for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema. Blocks bradykinin, the main driver of swelling, giving rapid relief from potentially life-threatening episodes.
mechanism: Competitively blocks bradykinin B2 receptors, preventing bradykinin-driven vasodilation, plasma leakage, and calcium-mediated nitric oxide synthase activation that causes edema in HAE attacks; synthetic modifications improve receptor specificity and stability.
safety: Injection-site reactions are very common (about 97%); transient fever and dizziness can occur, but it’s generally safe for rescue use.

name: IGF-1 DES (1-3)
evidence: Truncated analog of IGF-1 with high potency and short half-life. Primarily used in research settings for muscle growth.
primaryUse: Muscle growth and tissue regeneration enhancement
sideEffects: Potential growth of existing tissues including unwanted cell growth
summary: Truncated 67-amino-acid variant of IGF-1 from 1990s research, missing its first three amino acids, giving it about ten times the anabolic potency of regular IGF-1 with a short 20–30 minute half-life. Studied in animals for muscle growth, recovery, and tissue repair; remains an unapproved research chemical.
mechanism: Binds the IGF-1 receptor with much greater affinity than native IGF-1 due to reduced binding to IGF-binding proteins, strongly activating PI3K/Akt/mTOR and MAPK/ERK signaling to drive protein synthesis, cell proliferation, and satellite-cell activation in muscle and connective tissue.
safety: Hypoglycemia is a major risk; theoretical concern for tumor promotion and acromegaly-like tissue overgrowth with chronic use. Banned by WADA.

name: IGF-1 LR3
evidence: No FDA approval. Limited human clinical data (mostly anecdotal/gray market).
primaryUse: Muscle growth and tissue repair enhancement
sideEffects: Possible growth of existing tissues including unwanted growth
summary: Synthetic IGF-1 analog engineered for longer half-life and reduced binding to IGF-binding proteins, making it far more potent than natural IGF-1. Used in research on cell growth and differentiation, but widely misused in bodybuilding for muscle building.
mechanism: An arginine substitution and 13-amino-acid N-terminal extension cut IGF-binding-protein attachment and extend circulation time; acting through the IGF-1 receptor, it strongly drives PI3K/Akt/mTOR and MAPK/ERK signaling, boosting protein synthesis, amino acid uptake, and satellite-cell activity in muscle.
safety: High risk of hypoglycemia; potential for organ enlargement (acromegaly), insulin resistance, and cancer promotion. Not approved for human therapeutic use.

name: Insulin (various analogues: Lispro, Aspart, Glargine, Degludec, etc.)
evidence: FDA Approved. Extensive comparison studies (Degludec vs Glargine, etc.).
summary: Modified human insulin forms engineered for specific pharmacokinetics — rapid-acting types (Lispro, Aspart) mimic the after-meal insulin surge, while long-acting basal types (Glargine, Degludec) give a steady 24+ hour release. Central to modern diabetes management.
mechanism: Binds insulin receptors, triggering autophosphorylation and IRS activation that drives PI3K/Akt signaling (moving GLUT4 transporters to take up glucose, and blocking liver glucose production via FOXO inhibition) plus MAPK signaling for growth and protein synthesis; structural tweaks control how fast each analog is absorbed or forms stable depots.
safety: Hypoglycemia is the main risk; also injection-site reactions and weight gain, with long-term safety well established.

name: Ipamorelin
approval: Not FDA Approved. Re-evaluated by FDA in 2024 for potential compounding.
evidence: No active clinical trials. Previous Phase II trials for postoperative ileus were discontinued in the early 2000s due to lack of efficacy.
summary: Synthetic pentapeptide that selectively stimulates growth hormone release via the ghrelin receptor. Investigated in the 1990s for postoperative ileus, but Phase 2 trials were dropped for lack of efficacy; now mainly a research chemical with minimal recent clinical activity, though a 2024 FDA status review opened it to further compounding review without approving broader use.
mechanism: Selectively agonizes the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R) in the pituitary, raising intracellular calcium to trigger GH release via MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling, without stimulating cortisol, prolactin, or aldosterone, giving GH release patterns close to natural pulses.
safety: Generally well tolerated in studies, but long-term human safety is unknown.

name: JBSNF-000088 (6-Methoxynicotinamide)
evidence: Preclinical animal studies only.
summary: Orally active small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT), not a peptide. A 2018 study in obese mice found it reduced body weight, improved insulin sensitivity, and normalized glucose tolerance; remains a research compound.
mechanism: Blocks NNMT, lowering levels of the byproduct 1-methylnicotinamide, which in animal models is linked to improved insulin sensitivity, glucose control, and lower body weight.
safety: Limited data; research use only, with no human safety data available.

name: Keratin Peptides
evidence: Bioactive peptides derived from keratin. Used for hair/skin/nail health and as wound healing biomaterials.
primaryUse: Hair and skin structure enhancement and repair
summary: Bioactive fragments of natural keratin, the main structural protein in hair, skin, and nails, first studied in the 1940s. Used in cosmetics to strengthen keratin structures, improve moisture retention, and support skin/hair repair; not classified as drugs, with ongoing research into wound-healing uses.
mechanism: Penetrates skin and hair to act as building blocks and signals, stimulating keratin (K5, K14, K15) synthesis and collagen production via TGF-β signaling, while forming a protective scaffold and activating keratinocyte growth factor receptors for cell proliferation and repair.
safety: Excellent safety profile; non-toxic, non-irritating, biocompatible, and well tolerated orally.

name: Kisspeptin-10
evidence: Human studies for HSDD and fertility. Generally well-tolerated.
primaryUse: Reproductive hormone regulation and fertility enhancement
summary: Potent vasoconstrictor and anti-angiogenic peptide best known as a key regulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, triggering GnRH release and downstream LH/FSH secretion. Studied for infertility, psychosexual disorders, and possible cancer applications.
mechanism: Binds the GPR54 (KISS1R) receptor on hypothalamic GnRH neurons, activating Gq/11 and phospholipase C signaling to raise calcium and drive pulsatile GnRH release, which prompts pituitary LH and FSH secretion and downstream gonadal hormone production.
safety: Favorable profile with no major side effects reported in human studies; short half-life limits prolonged adverse effects.

name: KPV
evidence: Preclinical studies and limited human experimental use (topical/oral).
summary: C-terminal tripeptide fragment of alpha-MSH, studied for anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects. Investigated for colitis, psoriasis, and wound healing without the immunosuppressive downsides of steroids.
mechanism: Acts independently of melanocortin receptors to block pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) and NF-κB signaling in keratinocytes and immune cells, without triggering the pigmentation effects of its parent hormone α-MSH.
safety: Good safety profile in available studies; mild skin irritation topically and mild GI upset orally, but no long-term human data.

name: Lanreotide
evidence: FDA-approved Somatostatin analog (Somatuline). Standard of care for acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumors (NETs).
primaryUse: Treatment of acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumors
summary: Synthetic octapeptide analog of somatostatin from the 1980s, designed to outlast the natural hormone’s short half-life. Approved and widely used (Depot/Autogel) for acromegaly, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and carcinoid syndrome, with monthly dosing improving compliance over earlier analogs.
mechanism: Binds somatostatin receptors SSTR2 and SSTR5 with high affinity, triggering inhibitory G-protein signaling that cuts calcium influx and hormone release (GH, IGF-1, GI peptides); in neuroendocrine tumors it also curbs cell proliferation via PI3K/Akt suppression and reduces tumor blood vessel formation by lowering VEGF.
safety: GI disturbances (diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain) are very common; gallstones with prolonged use, injection-site nodules, and possible bradycardia or hyperglycemia.

name: Larazotide Acetate (INN-202)
evidence: Tight junction regulator reducing intestinal permeability ('leaky gut'). Investigational for Celiac disease adjunct therapy.
primaryUse: Treatment of celiac disease and intestinal permeability
summary: Peptide derived from a cholera toxin component (zonula occludens toxin), developed in the early 2000s to prevent intestinal tight-junction breakdown seen in celiac disease. In late-stage trials as a potential first drug specifically for celiac disease, aiming to reduce gluten-triggered symptoms and gut damage.
mechanism: Blocks the zonulin receptor PAR2, preventing zonulin-driven disassembly of tight-junction proteins (occludin, claudins, ZO-1), which keeps the gut barrier intact and limits gluten peptides from crossing into tissue, while also reducing MyD88-driven inflammatory signaling.
safety: Well tolerated in trials; adverse events (headache, UTI) similar to placebo, and its non-systemic action limits broader toxicity risk.

name: Lecanemab
evidence: Phase 3 (1,795 patients): 27% reduction in clinical decline vs placebo over 18 months
indication: Early Alzheimer's disease (MCI or mild dementia with confirmed amyloid)
summary: Humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody, accelerated FDA approval January 2023 and full approval July 2023, the first amyloid-targeting antibody fully approved for early Alzheimer’s. Targets the most neurotoxic soluble and insoluble amyloid-beta forms; its pivotal trial (1,795 participants) showed 27% slower decline over 18 months versus placebo.
mechanism: Binds and clears soluble amyloid-beta protofibrils and insoluble plaque forms, removing the most neurotoxic species.
safety: Boxed warning for ARIA, requiring MRI monitoring; most common effects are headache, infusion reactions, and ARIA.
boxedWarning: ARIA - risk of brain swelling and bleeding. MRI monitoring required

name: Leuprolide Acetate (Lupron, Eligard)
evidence: FDA-approved GnRH agonist. Standard of care for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, and central precocious puberty.
primaryUse: Hormone-dependent cancer and reproductive disorders treatment
summary: Synthetic GnRH agonist from 1985 (Lupron, Eligard), more potent and longer-lasting than natural GnRH. Approved for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty, available in daily, monthly, and extended-release forms.
mechanism: Initially stimulates LH/FSH release via Gq/11-coupled GnRH receptor activation, but continuous dosing desensitizes and internalizes the receptors, producing reversible medical castration by suppressing sex hormone production.
safety: Common effects include hot flashes, injection-site pain, and fatigue; serious risks include an initial tumor flare, bone density loss, metabolic syndrome, and depression or other psychiatric effects.

name: Linaclotide
evidence: Extensive Human Studies in adults. Recent Phase 2 and 3 trials have confirmed efficacy and safety in pediatric populations.
primaryUse: Treatment of chronic constipation and IBS-C
indication: Chronic Idiopathic Constipation, Irritable Bowel Syndrome with Constipation (IBS-C), Pediatric Functional Constipation
summary: 14-amino-acid guanylate cyclase-C receptor agonist, FDA-approved (2012) for chronic idiopathic constipation and IBS with constipation in adults, later expanded to pediatric constipation (2023, ages 6–17) and pediatric IBS-C (2025, ages 7–17). Works locally in the gut to boost fluid secretion, speed transit, and ease IBS-related abdominal pain.
mechanism: Activates guanylate cyclase-C receptors on intestinal cells, raising cGMP to activate the CFTR channel, driving chloride/bicarbonate secretion and water movement into the gut; elevated cGMP also reduces visceral pain signaling and dampens inflammatory cytokines.
safety: Good overall, but carries a boxed warning for pediatric use and commonly causes diarrhea.
boxedWarning: Risk of serious dehydration in pediatric patients; contraindicated in patients under 2 years of age.

name: Liraglutide (Victoza, Saxenda)
evidence: FDA Approved (Victoza, Saxenda).
summary: GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for type 2 diabetes (Victoza) and chronic weight management (Saxenda). Raises insulin release, lowers glucagon, and slows stomach emptying.
mechanism: Shares 97% sequence identity with human GLP-1; a palmitic acid side chain binds albumin, extending its half-life to about 13 hours. Receptor activation raises cAMP/PKA signaling for glucose-dependent insulin release, slows gastric emptying, and acts on hypothalamic neurons to increase satiety and reduce appetite.
safety: Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors (from rodent data); risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, and kidney impairment, plus common GI side effects.

name: Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala)
evidence: Used in Russia. Limited specific 'Livagen' clinical trials in Western databases (2020-2025).
primaryUse: Liver protection and immune system regulation
summary: Short synthetic peptide bioregulator (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) studied for modulating chromatin structure and gene expression, potentially reversing age-related DNA changes. Acts on immune, liver, and gut tissue, mainly researched in anti-aging and immune-normalization contexts.
mechanism: Interacts with nuclear factors in liver cells to shift gene expression toward anti-inflammatory cytokines over pro-inflammatory ones via JAK/STAT signaling, while supporting hepatocyte survival and regeneration through NF-κB-linked protective pathways and boosted detox enzyme expression.
safety: Considered safe as a bioregulator, with only theoretical mild side effects.

name: LL-37 (CAP-18)
evidence: Human Cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide. Promotes wound healing and modulates immunity. Investigational for venous leg ulcers.
summary: Naturally occurring 37-amino-acid antimicrobial peptide from the human cathelicidin family, discovered in 1995, active against bacteria, viruses, and fungi as part of innate immunity. Also promotes wound healing, resolves inflammation, and attracts immune cells; synthetic versions are being studied for resistant infections and chronic wounds.
mechanism: Disrupts microbial membranes via electrostatic attraction and pore formation; also binds FPRL1 and P2X7 receptors on immune cells to recruit neutrophils, monocytes, and T cells, activates dendritic cells via TLR signaling, aids epithelial migration through EGFR transactivation, and neutralizes bacterial endotoxin.
safety: Narrow therapeutic window due to toxicity at high concentrations; may worsen autoimmune conditions like psoriasis or lupus through inflammation. Topical use is safe; systemic use is limited by toxicity.

name: LTX-109
approval: Not FDA Approved. Has completed Phase 2 clinical trials.
evidence: Phase 2 trials completed for nasal decolonization, atopic dermatitis, and hidradenitis suppurativa.
summary: Synthetic antimicrobial peptidomimetic (Lytixar/Voxvoganan) from the early 2000s, developed for topical bacterial infections including MRSA. Studied for skin infections, wound care, and nasal decolonization of S. aureus; promising in Phase 2 trials but still in development.
mechanism: A positively charged structure electrostatically attaches to and disrupts bacterial membranes via pore formation, causing content leakage and cell death; selective for bacterial over mammalian membranes due to charge/composition differences, making resistance less likely than with conventional antibiotics.
safety: Favorable safety profile for topical use, with low systemic absorption.

name: Lutathera (Lutetium Lu 177 dotatate)
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
summary: Radiolabeled somatostatin analog (Lutetium Lu 177 dotatate) combining receptor-targeting with radioactive lutetium-177 for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. FDA-approved in 2018 for somatostatin receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, improving progression-free survival in patients who failed other treatments.
mechanism: The dotatate portion binds somatostatin receptor 2, overexpressed on neuroendocrine tumor cells; once internalized, lutetium-177’s beta radiation (penetrating up to 2mm) damages tumor DNA and causes cell death, while accompanying gamma emission allows imaging.
safety: Good.

name: Maridebart cafraglutide (AMG-133 / MariTide)
evidence: Antibody-peptide conjugate (GIP receptor antagonist and GLP-1 receptor agonist). Investigational for obesity with a long half-life allowing monthly dosing.
primaryUse: Weight management and metabolic disorder treatment
summary: Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist (AMG-133/MariTide) from Amgen, developed in the early 2020s with an Fc fusion for extended action allowing monthly dosing. In Phase 2 trials for obesity, showing notable weight loss and metabolic improvement.
mechanism: Activates GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells and hypothalamic neurons to boost insulin release, cut glucagon, and suppress appetite, while GIP receptor activation strengthens the incretin effect; the Fc fusion extends circulation via FcRn recycling for monthly dosing.
safety: GI effects (nausea, vomiting, constipation) are most common, mild to moderate and dose-dependent; no unexpected safety signals or major cardiac events reported in Phase 2.

name: Matrixyl (Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-3/4) & Matrixyl 3000 (Pal-GHK + Pal-GQPR/Rigin)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: Synthetic peptide complexes (Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-3/4, and enhanced Matrixyl 3000) developed by Sederma, launched starting 2000, designed to mimic skin’s natural repair processes. Boosts collagen and matrix protein production, shown to reduce wrinkle depth and improve texture; a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug.
mechanism: The palmitoyl group aids skin penetration, then activates fibroblasts via TGF-β/SMAD signaling to raise collagen I/III/IV, fibronectin, and hyaluronic acid; in Matrixyl 3000, Pal-GHK drives copper-dependent collagen cross-linking while Rigin modulates IL-6 and inflammation.
safety: Good.

name: Mazdutide (LY3305677 / IBI362)
evidence: Investigational GLP-1R and GCGR dual agonist. Shows significant weight loss and glycemic control in Type 2 diabetes and obesity trials.
primaryUse: Treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes
summary: Dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist (LY3305677/IBI362) discovered in 2018, combining GLP-1 and glucagon signaling for stronger metabolic effects than single-receptor drugs. In Phase 3 trials for obesity and type 2 diabetes, showing notable weight loss and glycemic improvement.
mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation boosts glucose-dependent insulin release, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and promotes satiety, while glucagon receptor activation raises energy expenditure and lipid metabolism; structural changes resist DPP-4 breakdown and bind albumin for once-weekly dosing.
safety: Mostly mild-to-moderate GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, vomiting), transient; some increased heart rate; low rate of serious adverse events, with no severe hypoglycemia in non-diabetics.

name: Melanostatin DM
evidence: Animal + In Vitro Studies
primaryUse: Research compound for interfering with melanin production.
summary: Synthetic peptide (also called MIF-1) derived from melanostatin, studied for its ability to inhibit alpha-MSH and reduce melanin production for lighter skin tone. Not FDA-approved; used as a research compound.
mechanism: Inhibits alpha-MSH, the hormone that drives melanin production, reducing tyrosinase enzyme activity and thereby melanin synthesis.
safety: Generally considered safe topically; animal research shows possible skin irritation, redness, rash, or temporary burning. Sold for research use only, not intended for human use.

name: Melanotan II (MT2)
evidence: Synthetic alpha-MSH analog. Promotes melanogenesis (tanning) and sexual arousal. widely used but unregulated.
primaryUse: Melanin production and skin tanning enhancement
summary: A synthetic analogue of α-MSH sold illicitly for tanning, with no approval from any major regulator. Case reports from 2020 flagged renal infarction, rhabdomyolysis, and kidney failure, making its use a public-health concern.
mechanism: Acts as a potent agonist at MC1R and MC4R; MC1R activation raises cAMP and tyrosinase activity, driving melanin production, while MC4R activation affects appetite and sexual-response pathways.
safety: Linked to kidney infarction, rhabdomyolysis, priapism, and possible melanoma risk, along with severe nausea and flushing.

name: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor, IGF-1Ec)
evidence: No specific human clinical trials found (2020-2025). Preclinical tissue repair studies.
summary: MGF, also known as IGF-1Ec, is an IGF-1 splice variant produced in muscle after mechanical strain or injury. It aids local repair and hypertrophy by activating satellite cells. Synthetic, often PEGylated, versions are used in muscle-regeneration research.
mechanism: Distinct from systemic IGF-1, it drives satellite-cell proliferation and migration via PI3K/Akt signaling and supports protein synthesis through mTOR, with expression peaking 24–72 hours after mechanical stimulation.
safety: Human safety data are absent; theoretical cancer risk is assumed by analogy with IGF-1.

name: Mifamurtide
evidence: Approved in Europe/Israel (Mepact). Not FDA approved.
summary: A synthetic analogue of muramyl dipeptide, a bacterial cell-wall fragment, that stimulates immune cells. Approved in Europe (Mepact) alongside chemotherapy after surgery for high-grade, non-metastatic osteosarcoma to lower recurrence risk.
mechanism: Binds NOD2 on monocytes and macrophages, raising TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-12 output and boosting macrophage and dendritic-cell activity against tumor cells, including recruitment of immune cells to the tumor site.
safety: Flu-like symptoms such as fever, chills, and fatigue are frequent; GI upset occurs; severe allergic reactions are rare.

name: MK-677 (Ibutamoren)
evidence: Orally active GH secretagogue. Increases GH and IGF-1. Investigational for sarcopenia but failed to gain approval due to safety/efficacy balance.
primaryUse: Growth hormone secretion enhancement and muscle preservation
summary: A non-peptide compound from the 1990s that mimics ghrelin to stimulate growth hormone and IGF-1 release through the pituitary's GHS-R receptor. Studied for lean mass, sleep, and bone density but never formally approved; still used as a research chemical.
mechanism: Binds GHS-R in the hypothalamus and pituitary, activating a G-protein pathway that raises calcium and PKC, amplifying GH pulses; its longer half-life than ghrelin gives sustained elevation over roughly a day.
safety: Raises risk of insulin resistance, high blood sugar, fluid retention, and increased appetite; carries an FDA heart-failure warning in some populations and is banned by WADA.

name: Motixafortide
evidence: GENESIS Phase 3 trial demonstrated superior stem cell mobilization vs placebo in combination with G-CSF
indication: Hematopoietic stem cell mobilization for autologous transplantation
summary: A 14-residue cyclic peptide CXCR4 blocker approved by the FDA in 2023 to mobilize blood stem cells for collection before autologous transplant in multiple myeloma. Combined with G-CSF, it produces fast, sustained release of stem cells into the blood.
mechanism: Binds CXCR4 with high affinity, blocking SDF-1α/CXCL12 and freeing bone-marrow-anchored stem cells into circulation.
safety: Generally well tolerated when used together with G-CSF.

name: MOTS-c
synonyms: Mitochondrial ORF of the 12S rRNA type-c
evidence: Mitochondrial-derived peptide (MDP). Regulates metabolic homeostasis and exercise mimetic effects. Investigational for obesity and longevity.
summary: A mitochondria-derived peptide that helps regulate metabolism, partly by moving to the nucleus to influence gene expression through AMPK. Preclinical work from 2020–2025 suggests possible benefit in gestational diabetes, ovarian cancer, hepatitis B, septic heart injury, and lung reperfusion injury, but it has not reached clinical use.
mechanism: Activates AMPK signaling and, under metabolic stress, enters the nucleus to affect metabolic genes; improves insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake in muscle and boosts mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation.
safety: Human safety is unestablished; theoretical risks include low blood sugar and mitochondrial overactivation, with injection-site reactions reported; banned by WADA at all times.

name: N-Acetyl Epithalon Amidate
evidence: Modified version of Epitalon with improved stability and blood-brain barrier penetration. Investigated for anti-aging, sleep regulation, and telomere maintenance.
summary: A 2000s modified version of Epithalon carrying an acetyl and amidate group meant to improve stability and bioavailability. It targets pineal function and melatonin output and is studied for telomerase activity, circadian regulation, and cellular repair, though human evidence is lacking and it remains a research compound.
