mechanism: Stimulates melatonin release from pinealocytes and SIRT1 expression, activates telomerase via hTERT upregulation, adjusts clock genes in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, and raises antioxidant enzymes for neuroprotection.
safety: Tolerability is inferred from Epithalon data and appears reasonable short term, but long-term safety and a theoretical telomerase-linked cancer risk are unknown; not FDA approved.

name: N-Acetyl Selank Amidate
approval: Not FDA Approved for human use. Sold for laboratory research use only.
evidence: Animal + In Vitro Studies
summary: A modified, acetylated and amidated version of the tuftsin-derived peptide Selank, designed for greater stability, potency, and brain penetration. Studied as a research compound for cognition, mood, and immune balance; not FDA-approved.
mechanism: Modulates GABA receptor activity and raises BDNF expression, stabilizes enkephalins for sustained calming and cognitive effects, and adjusts IL-6 and other inflammatory markers while affecting serotonin and norepinephrine turnover.
safety: Generally well tolerated, similar to standard Selank; occasional nasal irritation, headache, irritability, or dizziness reported; long-term data limited.

name: N-Acetyl Semax Amidate
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: An acetylated, amidated derivative of the Russian ACTH(4-10)-based peptide Semax, meant to improve stability and brain penetration. Animal studies suggest benefits for learning, memory, attention, and neuroprotection; unlike original Semax it holds no approval anywhere and is used only in research.
mechanism: Raises BDNF/TrkB signaling, engaging downstream PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways to support neuroplasticity genes; also modulates dopamine, serotonin, and glutamate activity and curbs microglial inflammation.
safety: Described as well tolerated, though independent human data are scarce.

name: NAD+ and its precursors NMN (Nicotinamide Mononucleotide) & NR (Nicotinamide Riboside)
evidence: NR has GRAS status. NMN/NR in clinical trials for aging, metabolic health, neurodegeneration.
primaryUse: Cellular energy production and anti-aging support
summary: NAD+ is a coenzyme central to energy metabolism that declines with age; NMN and NR are precursor supplements studied for restoring NAD+ levels, with proposed benefits for aging, metabolism, and neuroprotection.
mechanism: NMN and NR convert to NAD+ through the NAMPT/NMNAT salvage pathway; higher NAD+ activates sirtuins (SIRT1/3) that govern gene expression, DNA repair, and mitochondrial efficiency, and fuels PARP-driven DNA repair.
safety: Generally well tolerated; mild GI upset or flushing can occur; no severe short-term risks reported, though long-term human data are still accumulating.

name: Nesiritide
evidence: FDA approved for acute decompensated heart failure. Improves hemodynamics (reduces PCWP).
primaryUse: Treatment of acute decompensated heart failure
summary: A recombinant version of human B-type natriuretic peptide, FDA-approved in 2001 for acute decompensated heart failure. It causes vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis while damping the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; kidney and mortality concerns later narrowed its use to select, volume-overloaded patients.
mechanism: Binds natriuretic peptide receptor-A, raising cGMP and activating protein kinase G to relax vascular smooth muscle, lowering preload and afterload, increasing natriuresis, and suppressing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
safety: Hypotension is the main dose-limiting risk; kidney function needs monitoring; headache and nausea are common.

name: Nonapeptide-1 (Melanostatin-5)
evidence: Clinical studies on skin lightening/radiance (2020-2025). Used for hyperpigmentation.
primaryUse: Regulation of skin pigmentation and melanin production
summary: Also called Melanostatin-5, this biomimetic peptide blocks α-MSH from binding MC1R, curbing melanin production. It is used in cosmetic formulations to address hyperpigmentation and even out skin tone.
mechanism: Competitively blocks α-MSH at MC1R, lowering cAMP and tyrosinase activity to cut melanin synthesis, while also damping inflammatory cytokine and NF-κB signaling in skin cells.
safety: Well tolerated on skin; no major risks identified in cosmetic use.

name: Octreotide (Sandostatin)
evidence: FDA-approved Somatostatin analog. Standard of care for Acromegaly, Carcinoid syndrome, and VIPomas. Inhibits GH and various GI hormones.
primaryUse: Treatment of acromegaly and carcinoid syndrome
summary: A synthetic somatostatin mimic that suppresses growth hormone and other endocrine secretions. Long a mainstay for acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumor symptoms like carcinoid syndrome, it is now paired with radionuclide therapy as standard care for some advanced NETs, and used first-line for acute esophageal variceal bleeding.
mechanism: Binds somatostatin receptors, mainly SSTR2/5, lowering cAMP and calcium to suppress GH, IGF-1, and gut hormones, reduce splanchnic blood flow and motility, and slow tumor growth via cell-cycle arrest and reduced growth-factor signaling.
safety: Gallstones develop in a notable share of long-term users; GI upset is common; bradycardia and high blood sugar can occur.

name: Odevixibat
evidence: Phase 3 trial: 33% bile acid response vs 0% placebo. Significant pruritus reduction
sideEffects: Diarrhea or frequent bowel movements (31% vs 10% placebo)
summary: An IBAT-inhibiting drug approved by the FDA in 2021 for progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, giving the first non-surgical option to interrupt bile-acid recycling and reduce itching and serum bile-acid levels.
mechanism: Blocks the ileal bile acid transporter, interrupting enterohepatic circulation and boosting fecal bile-acid loss.
safety: Generally well tolerated; diarrhea is the most frequent side effect.

name: Oral amycretin (NNC0487-0111)
evidence: Oral co-agonist of GLP-1 and Amylin receptors. Demonstrated substantial weight loss (>13% in 12 weeks) in early trials.
summary: An oral GLP-1 receptor agonist (NNC0487-0111) engineered to survive digestion, aiming to match injectable GLP-1 drugs' benefits for glucose control and weight loss with pill convenience. Still in early clinical testing for type 2 diabetes and obesity, with promising but limited data so far.
mechanism: Activates pancreatic β-cell GLP-1 receptors to drive glucose-dependent insulin release and cut glucagon, while acting on hypothalamic receptors to curb appetite; structural modifications protect it from digestive enzymes.
safety: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are frequent, sometimes affecting most users, but typically mild to moderate; no distinct severe risks identified yet.

name: Orexin-A
approval: Not FDA approved as a drug; several dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) are FDA-approved for insomnia.
evidence: Animal + In Vitro Studies
primaryUse: Research compound for sleep-wake cycle regulation and metabolic control; its antagonists are used for insomnia.
sideEffects: Increased heart rate. (Note: Side effects for therapeutic antagonists may include next-morning drowsiness, impaired alertness, worsening of depression/suicidal thoughts, complex sleep behaviors.)
summary: Also known as hypocretin-1, this hypothalamic neuropeptide, discovered in 1998, governs wakefulness, appetite, and energy balance; its loss underlies narcolepsy. It is not itself an approved drug, but its receptor blockers are approved for insomnia.
mechanism: Acts on OX1R and OX2R receptors, mainly via Gq signaling that raises calcium and neuronal excitability; hypothalamic orexin neurons project to arousal centers, coordinating norepinephrine, histamine, and serotonin systems, and also link to feeding circuits.
safety: The natural peptide appears safe in research; its antagonist drugs can cause next-day drowsiness, reduced alertness, mood worsening, and complex sleep behaviors.

name: Orforglipron (LY3502970)
evidence: Oral, non-peptide small molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist. Investigational for obesity and Type 2 diabetes. Offers an oral alternative to injectables.
primaryUse: Oral treatment for diabetes and obesity
summary: An oral, once-daily, non-peptide small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes and obesity, offering a pill alternative to injected GLP-1 drugs. Trials through 2025 showed dose-dependent weight loss up to about 14.7% and better glucose control; it is now in Phase 3, including the ATTAIN weight-management program.
mechanism: Binds the GLP-1 receptor to raise cAMP and activate PKA, prompting glucose-dependent insulin release and less glucagon; also acts on hypothalamic neurons to cut appetite, slows stomach emptying via vagal signaling, and supports β-cell survival through PI3K/Akt.
safety: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are common but usually mild and temporary; no liver-toxicity signal has emerged, unlike some earlier oral GLP-1 candidates.

name: OS-01
evidence: Validated for skin rejuvenation and barrier repair. Shown to be safe for sensitive skin (eczema friendly) and effective in reducing cellular senescence markers.
summary: A synthetic peptide developed in 2019 for topical skincare, aimed at senescent skin cells and barrier health. Lab research suggests it activates longevity pathways, boosts collagen, and supports the skin barrier; it is sold in cosmetic lines but lacks large clinical trials.
mechanism: Regulates genes tied to skin barrier function and cellular senescence, lowering SASP factors while boosting autophagy and activating SIRT1/AMPK signaling to improve mitochondrial function and support ceramide and tight-junction gene expression.
safety: Strong topical safety profile with no reported systemic absorption; rare mild dryness or irritation; considered non-genotoxic.

name: Ovagen (Glu-Asp-Ala-Gly)
evidence: Synthetic tetrapeptide liver bioregulator. Used for liver support and metabolic regulation.
primaryUse: Immune system regulation and cellular protection
summary: A Russian-developed synthetic tetrapeptide (Glu-Asp-Ala-Gly) intended as a 'bioregulator' to support ovarian function. Studied within Russia but lacking recent research in major international databases; not FDA or EMA approved, and sold online as a supplement or research chemical.
mechanism: An immunomodulatory peptide acting through JAK/STAT signaling in T-lymphocytes and macrophages, raising anti-inflammatory cytokines and antioxidant defenses such as glutathione, while also affecting NF-κB signaling.
safety: Oral forms are generally described as well tolerated; unregulated injectable versions carry infection and contamination risk; robust human safety data are lacking.

name: Oxytocin
evidence: FDA approved for labor induction/PPH. Investigated for FTD, PTSD, pain (intranasal).
primaryUse: Labor induction and social bonding enhancement
summary: A hypothalamic neuropeptide hormone used clinically to induce labor and control postpartum bleeding. It is also studied intensively, often via nasal spray, for its roles in bonding and trust and for conditions like autism, PTSD, and anxiety.
mechanism: Binds oxytocin receptors, activating phospholipase C-β and calcium signaling to drive uterine and myoepithelial contraction; in the brain it modulates the amygdala and reward circuits, affecting trust and bonding, and sensitizes the uterus to prostaglandins during labor.
safety: Safe at doses used in obstetrics; high doses risk water intoxication or uterine rupture; nasal use is generally mild, with occasional dizziness or headache.

name: P21 (P021 / CNTF-derived peptide)
evidence: Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor (CNTF) mimetic. Enhances neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity. Investigational for Alzheimer's and cognitive decline.
summary: A 2010s synthetic peptide (P021) derived from CNTF, designed to mimic its cognitive and neuroprotective benefits while limiting the side effects of the full protein. Animal studies suggest gains in neurogenesis and cognition, but it remains in early research with no approved use.
mechanism: Activates BDNF/TrkB signaling along with PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways to support neuron survival, synaptic plasticity, and dendritic growth, and appears to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation and amyloid buildup.
safety: Human safety is unknown; animal data show good tolerability without the appetite loss seen with full-length CNTF; theoretical immunogenicity risk.

name: Pal-AHK (Palmitoyl Tripeptide-3)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A 1990s lipopeptide combining palmitic acid with a three-amino-acid sequence, developed for cosmetic anti-aging use. Marketed under names like Biopeptide CL to stimulate collagen and reduce fine lines, with cosmetic-level safety data but no therapeutic status.
mechanism: The palmitoyl tail aids skin penetration while the AHK sequence engages fibroblast receptors, activating SMAD-dependent TGF-β signaling to raise collagen gene expression and block collagen-degrading enzymes, alongside PI3K/Akt-driven fibroblast migration.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Pal-GHK (Palmitoyl Tripeptide-1 / Biopeptide CL)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A palmitoylated version of the natural GHK peptide from the 1990s, used in high-end cosmetics such as Biopeptide CL and Matrixyl 3000 to mimic TGF-β activity and boost collagen, fibronectin, and elastin production in skin.
mechanism: Its fatty-acid tail improves penetration, letting the peptide activate TGF-β/SMAD signaling that raises collagen and elastin genes while inhibiting matrix-degrading enzymes and promoting fibroblast survival via ERK1/2 and PI3K/Akt.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Palmitoyl Dipeptide-6
evidence: Used in cosmetic formulations for skin conditioning and barrier support. Exact clinical efficacy data for this specific sequence is sparse compared to Matrixyl peptides.
primaryUse: Skin rejuvenation and collagen production enhancement
summary: An early-2000s cosmetic peptide pairing two amino acids with palmitic acid to boost skin penetration and fibroblast collagen output. Used in premium skincare, though most evidence comes from manufacturer-backed studies.
mechanism: Engages fibroblast receptors to trigger TGF-β/SMAD signaling, raising Type I and III collagen while regulating matrix-degrading enzymes and showing mild anti-inflammatory NF-κB effects.
safety: Considered safe for cosmetic use at typical concentrations; no specific toxicology concerns reported.

name: Lipopeptide (Biopeptide EL / Palmitoyl Hexapeptide-12)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A Sederma lipopeptide from the early 2000s, marketed as Biopeptide EL, combining palmitic acid with a six-amino-acid sequence to improve skin absorption. It signals fibroblasts to raise collagen and elastin for better elasticity, though evidence is mostly company-sponsored.
mechanism: Engages TGF-β/SMAD signaling to raise collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycan output, while boosting integrin-mediated cell-matrix adhesion and guarding against matrix-degrading enzymes.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Palmitoyl Pentapeptide-4
evidence: The 'Gold Standard' anti-aging peptide. Stimulates collagen I, III, IV and fibronectin. Validated in numerous clinical studies for wrinkle reduction.
summary: Known commercially as Matrixyl, and combined with other peptides in Matrixyl 3000, this cosmetic peptide mimics natural skin-repair signals to raise collagen and other matrix proteins. Studies show reduced wrinkle depth and improved texture, though it remains a cosmetic rather than pharmaceutical ingredient.
mechanism: Penetrates via its palmitoyl tail and drives TGF-β/SMAD-dependent fibroblast activation, raising Collagen I, III, and IV, fibronectin, and hyaluronic acid; in the 3000 blend, added Pal-GHK and Rigin support collagen cross-linking and calm inflammation.
safety: Strong safety record; non-toxic, non-mutagenic, and non-carcinogenic, with minimal systemic absorption.

name: Pancragen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp)
evidence: Russian data. No FDA approval.
summary: A Russian-studied synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) intended to support and regenerate pancreatic tissue, explored for type 2 diabetes and pancreatitis through aiding cell differentiation and insulin secretion.
mechanism: Binds pancreatic cell receptors to activate PI3K/Akt and EGF-receptor signaling, supporting protein synthesis and repair, while reducing inflammatory cytokines via NF-κB modulation and aiding beta-cell function.
safety: No established human safety data outside Russia; presumed low toxicity.

name: Pasireotide
evidence: FDA approved (Signifor) for Cushing's disease and Acromegaly. Shows superior efficacy to first-generation SSAs in certain receptor profiles.
primaryUse: Treatment of Cushing's disease and acromegaly
summary: A cyclohexapeptide somatostatin analogue from the 2000s with broader receptor binding than octreotide, especially at sst5. Approved by the FDA and EMA for Cushing's disease unsuited to surgery, and for acromegaly with inadequate surgical response.
mechanism: Binds multiple somatostatin receptor subtypes, especially sst5, suppressing cAMP via G-protein signaling to curb ACTH secretion in Cushing's disease and GH/IGF-1 in acromegaly, aided by calcium-channel and phosphorylation effects.
safety: High blood sugar is the most common significant risk and needs monitoring; GI upset, gallstones, and QT prolongation are also concerns.

name: PE-22-28
evidence: Preclinical only. No significant human clinical trials found.
summary: A synthetic derivative of the spadin peptide that blocks TREK-1 channels, studied for possible antidepressant effects through stimulating neurogenesis and mood regulation. It remains a research chemical with no human trial data.
mechanism: Crosses the blood-brain barrier to engage BDNF/TrkB signaling, promoting synaptic plasticity, dendritic growth, and long-term potentiation, aided by cAMP/PKA activity and reduced oxidative and inflammatory markers.
safety: No human safety data exist; animal studies suggest low toxicity but possible CNS effects such as sedation or irritability.

name: PEG-MGF
evidence: No specific human clinical trials found (2020-2025). Preclinical tissue repair studies.
sideEffects: Potential impact on blood sugar levels
summary: A PEGylated form of MGF (IGF-1Ec), the IGF-1 splice variant induced by muscle strain, used in research to extend the compound's activity for studying muscle repair and hypertrophy.
mechanism: Works through the IGF-1 receptor with a focus on satellite-cell activation; PEGylation extends its half-life, sustaining PI3K/Akt/mTOR-driven protein synthesis, satellite-cell fusion, and VEGF-mediated local blood-vessel growth.
safety: Human safety data are absent; theoretical cancer risk mirrors that of IGF-1.

name: Pegulicianine
evidence: INSITE Phase 3 (406 patients): 84% diagnostic accuracy in detecting residual cancer real-time
indication: Intraoperative fluorescence imaging of residual breast cancer
summary: An FDA-approved (2024) fluorescent imaging agent used during breast-cancer surgery to spot residual tumor tissue after lumpectomy. It stays dark until tumor-associated enzymes activate it, and paired with the Lumicell system it reached about 84% diagnostic accuracy in the Phase 3 INSITE trial.
mechanism: An inactive prodrug linking a fluorophore and quencher is cleaved by tumor-overexpressed cathepsins and matrix metalloproteinases, separating the two components and producing a fluorescent signal in cancerous tissue.
safety: Well tolerated for its imaging role.

name: Pemvidutide (ALT-801)
evidence: Investigational GLP-1/Glucagon dual agonist. Shows robust weight loss and significant reduction in liver fat (MASH).
primaryUse: Obesity and fatty liver disease treatment
summary: An early-2020s dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist (ALT-801) engineered for an extended half-life, aimed at obesity and fatty liver disease. Phase 2 data show encouraging reductions in liver fat, weight, and glucose markers.
mechanism: GLP-1 activation raises insulin release and appetite suppression while cutting glucagon; simultaneous glucagon-receptor activation raises energy expenditure and liver fat oxidation; a linker technology sustains receptor engagement.
safety: Nausea and vomiting are the most common effects, generally mild to moderate and dose-related; no notable rise in heart rate or major cardiac events seen in trials.

name: Pentapeptide-18 (Leuphasyl)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
primaryUse: Reduction of expression lines and wrinkles
summary: Known as Leuphasyl, this early-2000s cosmetic peptide was designed as a gentler alternative to botulinum toxin for reducing expression lines, often combined with Argireline. Manufacturer studies show reduced muscle-contraction intensity, but independent clinical research is limited.
mechanism: Mimics enkephalins to bind nerve-terminal receptors and reduce acetylcholine release, interfering with SNARE-complex-driven vesicle fusion and thereby lowering the frequency and force of facial muscle contractions.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Pinealon (Glu-Asp-Arg)
evidence: Short peptide bioregulator (tripeptide). Investigated for neuroprotective effects and gene expression modulation.
summary: A 1990s Russian-developed tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) designed to cross the blood-brain barrier and support cognition and neuroprotection. Animal studies suggest memory and learning benefits, but research remains mostly confined to Russia and Eastern Europe with limited human trials.
mechanism: Stimulates BDNF expression and TrkB signaling, engaging PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways for neuron survival and plasticity, while helping regulate calcium balance, oxidative stress, and genes tied to neuroplasticity.
safety: Appears benign in available studies; possible mild effects include vivid dreams, GI upset, or mood shifts; long-term human data are limited.

name: Plecanatide
evidence: FDA approved (Trulance). Guanylate cyclase-C agonist effective for chronic idiopathic constipation and IBS-C.
primaryUse: Treatment of chronic idiopathic constipation and IBS-C
summary: A synthetic analogue of the gut peptide uroguanylin, FDA-approved in 2017 for chronic idiopathic constipation and IBS with constipation. It mimics natural GI signaling with minimal systemic absorption, suiting it to long-term use.
mechanism: Activates guanylate cyclase-C receptors on intestinal cells, raising cGMP that opens CFTR channels to boost chloride and bicarbonate secretion and draw water into the gut, softening stool; works best in the acidic upper small intestine.
safety: Diarrhea is the most common side effect, around 4%; generally well tolerated; rare risk of serious dehydration in children under 6, in whom it's contraindicated.

name: Pluvicto (Lutetium Lu 177 vipivotide tetraxetan)
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
primaryUse: Treatment of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
summary: A targeted radiopharmaceutical pairing a PSMA-binding molecule with radioactive lutetium-177, approved by the FDA in 2022 for PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after prior treatment. It marked a major step for precision nuclear medicine in oncology.
mechanism: Binds PSMA overexpressed on prostate cancer cells, delivering localized beta radiation with about a 1 mm range that causes DNA breaks and cell death in tumor and nearby cells, with a stable chelator preventing systemic release of the isotope.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: PNC-27 / PNC-28
evidence: No FDA approval. No published human clinical trials. FDA warning issued in 2017.
summary: Synthetic peptides derived from p53 designed to bind HDM-2 on cancer cells and trigger pore formation and cell death. Preclinical data suggest selective cancer-cell killing, but there is no human clinical evidence, and the FDA has warned against their use.
mechanism: A cell-penetrating domain lets these peptides reach HDM2 overexpressed on cancer-cell membranes, where binding causes pore formation and necrotic death rather than working through intracellular p53 signaling as typical p53-based therapies do.
safety: Human safety is unknown; selectivity claims come only from preclinical work, and the FDA has warned of contamination risks with sold products.

name: Pramlintide
evidence: Extensive Human Studies
primaryUse: Adjunct to insulin therapy for type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
indication: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (as adjunct to insulin).
summary: A synthetic amylin analogue, marketed as Symlin and FDA-approved in 2005 as an add-on to insulin for type 1 and type 2 diabetes. It slows gastric emptying, curbs post-meal glucagon, and boosts satiety, and remains the only approved drug in its class.
mechanism: Binds amylin receptors in the brainstem and hypothalamus to slow stomach emptying and cut glucagon secretion via calcitonin-receptor pathways, working alongside insulin to limit liver glucose output and enhance satiety through area postrema and vagal signaling.
safety: Notable risk of severe hypoglycemia with insulin, requiring dose adjustment; avoided in gastroparesis, hypoglycemia unawareness, or high HbA1c; nausea, vomiting, appetite loss, fatigue, headache, and dizziness are common.

name: Prostamax (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro)
evidence: Preclinical/Russian data. No FDA approval or Western clinical trials found.
summary: A synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro) studied as a bioregulator for prostate health, aimed at reducing inflammation and supporting gland function in conditions like BPH or prostatitis by influencing gene expression in prostate tissue.
mechanism: Modulates androgen-receptor signaling and prostate cell growth, acting through membrane receptors that trigger pathways controlling inflammation and tissue-specific protein synthesis, including PI3K/Akt and PSA-related transcription factors.
safety: Human safety data are lacking; presumed low toxicity based on its peptide class.

name: Protirelin (TRH - Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone)
evidence: Diagnostic use. Investigated for neurodegenerative diseases and depression.
primaryUse: Neurological enhancement and thyroid function testing
summary: A synthetic analogue of thyrotropin-releasing hormone used mainly as a diagnostic tool for thyroid function testing. Neurotrophic uses for spinal cord injury or depression are studied but limited by rapid breakdown and poor brain penetration.
mechanism: Binds TRH receptors in the pituitary and CNS, activating the PLC/IP/PKC cascade to raise calcium and trigger TSH and prolactin release; centrally it boosts cholinergic, noradrenergic, and dopaminergic signaling, with possible antidepressant and neuroprotective effects.
safety: Generally safe; transient nausea, dizziness, or agitation can occur with intravenous use.

name: PT-141 (Bremelanotide / Vyleesi)
evidence: FDA approved for Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder (HSDD) in premenopausal women. Effective melanocortin receptor agonist.
primaryUse: Treatment of hypoactive sexual desire disorder
summary: Also called Bremelanotide (Vyleesi), this melanocortin receptor agonist developed from Melanotan II gained FDA approval in 2019 for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women, only the second approved drug for that condition, and works through the brain rather than blood flow.
mechanism: Selectively activates MC4R in the central nervous system, engaging G-protein signaling that raises cAMP and PKA activity, altering neurotransmitter release in the hypothalamus and limbic system to boost sexual motivation via dopaminergic and adrenergic pathways.
safety: Nausea is very common, around 40%; flushing and headache occur; transient blood pressure rises can occur; frequent use risks permanent focal hyperpigmentation.

name: PTD-DBM
evidence: Preclinical only. No confirmed human trials (2020-2025).
summary: A synthetic peptide designed to activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling by blocking CXXC5, studied mainly for hair regrowth and wound-triggered hair regeneration, often applied topically alongside valproic acid.
mechanism: A cell-penetrating domain lets it reach the nucleus, where it disrupts Smad1 interactions to influence BMP signaling, raising BDNF and supporting neuron survival, plasticity, and reduced oxidative and inflammatory stress in neural tissue.
safety: Human safety data are lacking; sold as a 'cosmetic' in some markets; theoretical cancer risk tied to Wnt pathway activation.

name: Retatrutide
evidence: Phase 3 trials ongoing (TRIUMPH program). Phase 2 data published in NEJM showing significant efficacy.
primaryUse: Treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes
summary: A triple agonist (LY3437943) hitting GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors, developed by Eli Lilly. Trial data show strong weight loss and glucose control, exceeding many dual agonists; it is in Phase 3 testing for obesity and type 2 diabetes.
mechanism: GLP-1 activation drives glucose-dependent insulin release and satiety; GIP activation improves insulin sensitivity and nutrient storage; glucagon-receptor activation raises energy expenditure and fat metabolism, together producing added metabolic effect; structural changes allow once-weekly dosing.
safety: Profile similar to other incretin drugs; nausea and diarrhea are common and dose-related; a transient heart-rate increase has been observed.

name: Rezafungin
evidence: Phase 3 study demonstrated non-inferiority to comparator echinocandin with primary endpoint of day 30 all-cause mortality
sideEffects: Similar to other echinocandins - generally well tolerated
summary: A semisynthetic echinocandin antifungal approved by the FDA in 2023, the first new candidemia/invasive candidiasis treatment in over a decade. Its long half-life, over 130 hours, allows once-weekly dosing instead of the daily treatment used by other echinocandins.
mechanism: Inhibits 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase, an enzyme Candida species need to build their cell wall.
safety: Safety profile similar to other echinocandins; not studied for endocarditis, osteomyelitis, or meningitis caused by Candida.

name: Rigin (Palmitoyl Tetrapeptide-7)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: Also called Palmitoyl Tetrapeptide-7, this early-2000s cosmetic peptide targets skin inflammation and aging by lowering interleukin-6 output. Lab studies show reduced inflammatory markers and improved collagen synthesis, though it remains a cosmetic rather than therapeutic ingredient.
mechanism: Its palmitoyl group aids skin penetration while the peptide portion curbs UV- and stimulus-triggered IL-6 overproduction, lowering matrix-metalloproteinase activity and helping maintain balanced collagen turnover and glycosaminoglycan synthesis.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Romidepsin
evidence: FDA approved for CTCL. PTCL indication withdrawn in 2021.
summary: An HDAC inhibitor, marketed as Istodax, approved by the FDA for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma after at least one prior systemic therapy. It alters gene expression tied to cell-cycle arrest and death, killing cancer cells.
mechanism: After cellular uptake, a released thiol group chelates zinc in the HDAC active site, raising histone acetylation to boost tumor-suppressor and cell-cycle genes; this triggers p21-driven cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis via death receptors, disrupted DNA repair, and enhanced immune recognition of tumor cells.
safety: Can cause blood-cell toxicity, GI issues, and fatigue; serious infections are possible; ECG T-wave changes can occur.

name: Rusfertide
approval: Phase 3 Clinical Trial (Breakthrough Therapy Designation granted August 2025)
evidence: Phase 3 VERIFY study met its primary endpoint for polycythemia vera. Positive Phase 2 REVIVE trial results also published.
primaryUse: Treatment of polycythemia vera and iron disorders
summary: An investigational hepcidin-mimicking peptide for polycythemia vera, holding FDA Breakthrough Therapy, Orphan Drug, and Fast Track status. The Phase 3 VERIFY trial met its main goal by cutting the need for phlebotomy, with an NDA filing expected by the end of 2025.
mechanism: Binds ferroportin, the cell's iron-export channel, triggering its internalization and breakdown via JAK/STAT-driven phosphorylation and ubiquitination, which lowers serum iron and limits excess red blood cell production.
safety: Generally well tolerated in trials; injection-site reactions are the most common adverse event.

name: SCO-094
evidence: Investigational dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist. Developed for Type 2 Diabetes, Obesity, and NASH. Shows potential for significant weight loss.
primaryUse: Skin regeneration and collagen synthesis enhancement
summary: An early-2010s synthetic peptide studied for dermatology, aimed at boosting collagen synthesis and skin regeneration. Preliminary lab work suggests effects on fibroblast activity and Type I/III collagen, but it remains in early research with no approved use.
mechanism: Binds dermal fibroblast receptors to trigger TGF-β/SMAD signaling, raising collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycan output while inhibiting matrix-degrading enzymes; also promotes keratinocyte renewal via EGFR pathway activation.
safety: Early trials describe it as well tolerated, with GI-type effects reported; no severe drug-related signals reported so far.

name: Selank
approval: Approved in Russia for GAD and as a nootropic; Not FDA Approved in US/Western countries.
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A Russian-developed synthetic heptapeptide derived from tuftsin, used as an anxiolytic, nootropic, and neuroprotective agent by adjusting GABA signaling, serotonin, dopamine, and BDNF, and by blocking enkephalin breakdown. Approved in Russia for generalized anxiety and as a nootropic; a research compound elsewhere.
mechanism: Modulates BDNF and serotonin metabolism and T-helper lymphocyte balance, crosses the blood-brain barrier to enhance GABA-driven inhibitory signaling for calming effects without sedation, and blocks enkephalinase to preserve natural regulatory peptides, normalizing noradrenaline and serotonin in memory-related brain regions.
safety: Generally better tolerated than standard anxiolytics, without drowsiness, dependence, or withdrawal; occasional headache, local irritation, sore throat, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, or anxiety; long-term data outside Russia are limited.

name: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy)
evidence: FDA Approved (Ozempic, Wegovy). SELECT trial data.
summary: A long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist approved as Ozempic and oral Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for weight management. It has driven major gains in obesity treatment, though GI side effects require gradual dose increases.
mechanism: Shares most of native GLP-1's sequence and activates its receptor via cAMP signaling, boosting glucose-dependent insulin release and curbing glucagon; a fatty-acid modification extends its half-life to about a week by binding albumin and resisting breakdown; centrally it lowers appetite and slows gastric emptying, with added cardiovascular and anti-inflammatory effects.
safety: GI side effects are common; gallbladder risk exists; rare pancreatitis or bowel obstruction; an emerging signal for a vision condition, NAION, has been noted.

name: Semax
approval: Approved as prescription drug in Russia and Eastern Europe; Not FDA Approved in US/EU.
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A Russian- and Eastern European-used synthetic heptapeptide derived from ACTH(1-7), valued for nootropic, neuroprotective, and neurorestorative effects via BDNF upregulation and neurotransmitter modulation. Approved clinically in Russia; a research chemical in the US, EU, and most other markets.
mechanism: Offers greater stability and brain penetration than natural ACTH(4-10), raising BDNF/TrkB signaling and serotonin/dopamine levels while regulating glutamate; activates MAPK/ERK to support synaptic growth and neuron survival, and lowers inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress in the CNS.
safety: Generally well tolerated; most side effects are mild and tied to nasal use; may raise blood glucose in diabetics; not for use in pregnancy or breastfeeding; long-term effects largely unknown.

name: Sermorelin (Geref)
approval: FDA approved (1997), but commercially discontinued in 2008. Available via compounding pharmacies.
evidence: Extensive Human Studies prior to 2008. A 2021 study showed benefits in an animal model of heart failure.
primaryUse: Stimulation of natural growth hormone production
summary: A 29-amino-acid GHRH analogue, the shortest fully active GHRH fragment, approved by the FDA in the 1990s for pediatric growth hormone deficiency and diagnostics, then discontinued commercially in 2008 for business reasons, not safety. It prompts natural pulsatile GH release and remains available through compounding pharmacies, often for off-label age-management use.
mechanism: Binds GHRH receptors on pituitary somatotrophs, raising cAMP via adenylate cyclase to trigger PKA activity, calcium influx, and GH vesicle release; it also upregulates GHRH receptor expression, preserving natural GH pulsing patterns.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Setmelanotide
evidence: Demonstrated significant weight loss in Phase 3 trials for patients with POMC and LEPR deficiency
primaryUse: Chronic weight management in genetic obesity (POMC, PCSK1, LEPR deficiency, Bardet-Biedl syndrome)
indication: Genetic obesity (POMC, PCSK1, or LEPR deficiency)
summary: A first-in-class MC4R agonist, FDA-approved in 2020 for chronic weight management in adults and children six and older with obesity caused by POMC, PCSK1, or LEPR deficiency. This cyclic octapeptide crosses the blood-brain barrier to restore hypothalamic appetite control.
mechanism: Activates melanocortin receptors MC4R, MC3R, and MC1R in the hypothalamus, restoring signaling in the melanocortin pathway that governs appetite and energy use.
safety: Common effects include injection-site reactions and hyperpigmentation; serious risks include depression, suicidal thoughts, and sexual side effects.

name: SLU-PP-332
evidence: Preclinical only. No human trials found (2020-2025).
summary: A novel synthetic agonist targeting estrogen-related receptors alpha, beta, and gamma, often described as an 'exercise mimetic' for its potential to raise metabolic endurance and preserve muscle function without exercise. It remains in preclinical development.
safety: Animal studies indicate good safety, without liver or kidney toxicity; a theoretical risk of cardiac hypertrophy via ERR-gamma activation exists.

name: SNAP-8 (Acetyl Octapeptide-3)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
primaryUse: Reduction of expression wrinkles and fine lines
summary: Also called Acetyl Octapeptide-3, this cosmetic peptide was designed as a gentler alternative to botulinum toxin, modeled on the SNAP-25 protein sequence to reduce muscle-contraction-driven wrinkles, particularly on the forehead and around the eyes. Lab studies suggest roughly 30% of Botox's wrinkle-reducing effect, though independent clinical trials are limited.
mechanism: Competes with SNAP-25 to destabilize the VAMP/SNAP-25/Syntaxin complex needed for neurotransmitter vesicle fusion, reducing acetylcholine release and calcium-dependent muscle contraction in facial muscles; also promotes fibroblast collagen production.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: SS-31 (Elamipretide / Bendavia)
evidence: FDA Accelerated Approval (Forzinity) for Barth Syndrome (2025). Phase 3 trials for PMM and dry AMD.
primaryUse: Mitochondrial function enhancement in cardiovascular disease
summary: Known as Elamipretide, this tetrapeptide binds cardiolipin on the inner mitochondrial membrane to stabilize mitochondrial structure and support ATP production. It recently gained FDA accelerated approval, as Forzinity, for Barth syndrome, a rare mitochondrial genetic disorder.
mechanism: Its alternating aromatic-cationic sequence lets it concentrate heavily in mitochondria, where cardiolipin binding blocks damaging cytochrome c peroxidase activity and stabilizes cristae structure, improving electron transport chain efficiency, lowering reactive oxygen species, and preserving membrane potential and fusion/fission balance, especially during ischemia-reperfusion stress.
safety: Injection-site reactions are common, around 80% of users; otherwise generally well tolerated.

name: Survodutide (BI 456906)
evidence: Phase 3 trials ongoing (SYNCHRONIZE). Strong weight loss and liver fat reduction data.
primaryUse: Treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes
summary: A dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist (BI 456906) from Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma. It combines glucagon-driven energy expenditure with GLP-1-driven appetite suppression for weight management and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis.
mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation raises glucose-dependent insulin release, cuts glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and promotes satiety via the hypothalamus; glucagon receptor activation adds energy expenditure and fat oxidation through liver glucose production and thermogenesis; structural modifications extend its half-life.
safety: GI effects such as nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting are common and dose-related; some trials saw higher discontinuation due to GI issues.

name: Syn-AKE (Dipeptide Diaminobutyroyl Benzylamide Diacetate)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A 2006 synthetic tripeptide mimicking Waglerin-1 from temple viper venom, designed as a safer topical alternative to botulinum toxin for facial lines. Studies report up to about 52% reduced wrinkle depth after 28 days, though evidence is largely from cosmetic trials rather than rigorous clinical research.
mechanism: Reversibly blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, reducing acetylcholine-driven muscle contraction and calcium channel activity, producing temporary muscle relaxation without full paralysis; also supports dermal matrix protein synthesis.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Syn-Coll (Palmitoyl Tripeptide-5)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
primaryUse: Stimulation of collagen synthesis in skin
summary: Known as Palmitoyl Tripeptide-5, this early-2000s cosmetic peptide mimics the body's TGF-β-driven collagen production pathway. Lab studies show increased collagen output and organization in skin fibroblasts, though evidence is mainly from manufacturer-sponsored research.
mechanism: Mimics TGF-β's receptor-binding domain to trigger SMAD2/3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, raising transcription of collagen genes COL1A1 and COL3A1, and helping regulate matrix-degrading enzymes; its palmitoyl tail aids skin penetration.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4) (and its active fragment Ac-SDKP)
evidence: Full-length T-beta-4 has trials. TB-500 (fragment) has none.
sideEffects: Temporary hair growth at injection site
summary: A synthetic peptide fragment of Thymosin Beta-4, sold widely as a research chemical for injury recovery even though only the full-length protein has entered clinical trials for wound healing and cardiac repair. It promotes cell migration and blood-vessel growth but lacks formal human safety data and is banned in sports.
mechanism: Acts as a G-actin-sequestering protein regulating actin assembly and cell migration, raises VEGF and bFGF to spur blood-vessel growth and repair, and its active Ac-SDKP fragment blocks TGF-β signaling to limit heart fibrosis; also engages the ILK-PINCH-PARVA complex and PI3K/Akt pathway to protect heart cells under low-oxygen stress and aid stem-cell migration to injury sites.
safety: Full Thymosin Beta-4 is safe in trials, but this shorter form lacks human safety data; it is WADA-banned and carries a theoretical cancer risk.

name: TB-500 Fragment (17-23) (Ac-SDKP)
evidence: Full-length T-beta-4 has trials. TB-500 (fragment) has none.
primaryUse: Prevention and treatment of cardiovascular fibrosis
summary: A synthetic fragment (amino acids 17-23) of Thymosin Beta-4, sold widely as a research chemical for injury recovery even though only the full-length protein has entered clinical trials for wound healing and heart repair. It promotes cell migration and blood-vessel growth but lacks formal human safety data and is banned in sports.
mechanism: The active fragment, Ac-SDKP, blocks TGF-β signaling in heart and kidney tissue by inhibiting Smad2/3 activation, reducing fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and collagen buildup, while curbing inflammation via reduced macrophage infiltration and NF-κB signaling and supporting cell survival through PI3K/Akt.
safety: Full Thymosin Beta-4 is safe in trials, but this shorter fragment lacks human safety data; it is WADA-banned and carries a theoretical cancer risk.

name: Teduglutide
approval: FDA Approved (2012 for adults, 2019 for pediatrics); EMA Approved (2012)
evidence: Extensive Human Studies, including Phase 3 clinical trials in both adult and pediatric populations with short bowel syndrome. It is an established therapy recommended in international clinical guidelines for malabsorption.
summary: A recombinant analogue of GLP-2, approved by the FDA and EMA for short bowel syndrome in patients needing parenteral support, for adults since 2012 and children one and older since 2019. It promotes intestinal-lining growth and better nutrient absorption; 2024 pediatric data confirm sustained benefit over 96 weeks, and preclinical work hints at use in graft-versus-host disease.
mechanism: A single amino-acid substitution extends its half-life versus native GLP-2; it binds GLP-2 receptors on gut cells to raise crypt-cell growth, reduce cell death, boost blood flow via nitric oxide, and expand villus height and absorptive surface, while raising nutrient transporters and digestive enzyme secretion.
safety: Generally well tolerated with monitoring; requires a formal risk management program due to serious potential risks.
boxedWarning: Increased risk of malignancies, intestinal obstruction, gallbladder disease, biliary tract disease, and pancreatic disease.

name: Teriparatide (Forteo)
evidence: FDA Approved (Forteo) for osteoporosis.
primaryUse: Treatment of severe osteoporosis and fracture prevention
summary: A recombinant fragment, amino acids 1-34, of human parathyroid hormone, marketed as Forteo and FDA-approved as a bone-building treatment for osteoporosis in men and postmenopausal women at high fracture risk.
mechanism: Binds PTH1R on bone-building cells; given intermittently, it favors bone formation over resorption by activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling and suppressing sclerostin, boosting osteoblast activity and survival and raising local IGF-1 to support bone matrix production.
safety: The osteosarcoma boxed warning was removed in 2020; risks include high blood calcium and low blood pressure on standing; use is limited to two years.

name: Terlipressin
evidence: CONFIRM trial: significant improvement in HRS reversal (55% vs 4.8% midodrine-octreotide)
summary: A synthetic vasopressin analogue selective for V1 receptors, FDA-approved in 2022 as the first drug specifically for improving kidney function in hepatorenal syndrome. It lowers portal pressure and improves renal blood flow, given for up to 14 days or until kidney function markers normalize.
mechanism: Selectively activates V1 receptors, reducing portal pressure and raising effective blood volume and arterial pressure, which improves the kidneys' filtration rate.
safety: Serious risks include respiratory failure, requiring continuous oxygen monitoring; avoided in patients with heart dysfunction or fluid overload.
boxedWarning: Risk of respiratory failure. Continuous monitoring required

name: Tesamorelin (Egrifta)
evidence: FDA Approved (Egrifta).
summary: A synthetic GHRH analogue, marketed as Egrifta and FDA-approved to reduce excess abdominal fat in HIV patients with lipodystrophy, by prompting the pituitary to release growth hormone that acts on fat tissue.
mechanism: Binds GHRH receptors on pituitary cells to stimulate GH synthesis and release, raising IGF-1 and promoting fat breakdown especially in visceral fat, with structural changes giving it greater stability and half-life than natural GHRH while preserving receptor specificity.
safety: Injection-site reactions and hypersensitivity can occur; risk of glucose intolerance or diabetes; raises IGF-1, requiring cancer monitoring.

name: Testagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly)
evidence: Russian studies. No FDA approval.
primaryUse: Male reproductive system and testosterone support
summary: A synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly) 'bioregulator' studied for male reproductive health, aimed at normalizing testosterone, sperm quality, and sexual function by influencing gene expression in the testes.
mechanism: Enhances signaling along the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, raising LH and FSH release to boost testosterone production in Leydig cells and support sperm production in Sertoli cells, partly via increased StAR protein expression and antioxidant protection of reproductive tissue.
safety: Generally described as safe within its bioregulator class; mild side effects reported.

name: Thymalin
evidence: Used in Russia/Eastern Europe for decades. Recent studies for COVID-19 adjunct therapy.
summary: A Russian-developed polypeptide complex from thymus tissue, valued for immune-modulating effects that balance T- and B-lymphocyte ratios and boost cellular immunity. Used clinically in Eastern Europe for immune deficiencies and infections, and studied recently as an adjunct for severe COVID-19.
mechanism: Promotes T-lymphocyte maturation in the thymus and peripheral tissue, raises thymic hormone output, and modulates cytokines like IL-2 and IFN-γ; helps normalize T-helper/T-suppressor ratios, boosts NK-cell activity, and shows anti-inflammatory effects via JAK/STAT regulation.
safety: Good safety profile in available studies; minimal side effects such as localized redness.

name: Thymogen
evidence: Limited to Russian studies; no recent, large-scale clinical trials found in major international databases.
summary: A Russian-developed synthetic dipeptide (Glu-Trp), also called Thymagen, used there as an immune-modulating 'bioregulator,' including for viral infections and dental disease. Recent large-scale international clinical data are lacking; not FDA or EMA approved and sold online as a research chemical.
mechanism: Promotes immature T-cell maturation in the thymus, raising CD3+/CD4+ marker expression and adjusting the CD4+/CD8+ ratio; believed to bind DNA and nuclear proteins to activate JAK/STAT signaling, increasing IL-2 and IFN-γ output, boosting NK-cell and macrophage activity, and reducing inflammation via NF-κB modulation.
safety: Reported as well tolerated with low toxicity in Russian use, but not confirmed by large modern Western clinical trials.

name: Thymosin Alpha-1 (Zadaxin)
evidence: Thymic peptide immunomodulator. Enhances T-cell function. Approved in many countries (not US) for Hepatitis B/C and as a vaccine adjuvant.
primaryUse: Immune system enhancement and viral infection treatment
summary: A synthetic 28-amino-acid peptide matching a natural thymic hormone, marketed as Zadaxin. It's an established immune modulator approved in many countries for hepatitis B and C, as a cancer-therapy adjuvant, and for immune-compromised patients. Since 2020, interest has grown in its use for COVID-19 and long COVID, boosting antitumor immunity in lung cancer, and for immune support in severe acute pancreatitis.
mechanism: Binds Toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR9 to drive T-cell maturation and Th1 cytokine output, raises MHC class I expression and dendritic-cell maturation, boosts NK-cell and antibody activity, and activates NF-κB and MyD88-dependent signaling to strengthen immune response against viruses and cancer while reducing inflammation.
safety: Excellent safety record; adverse events are rare and usually mild, such as injection-site reactions; no significant drug-related toxicity seen in large trials.

name: Thymulin (Thymic Factor)
approval: Not FDA approved as a drug. Rethymic (related product) approved for congenital athymia (2021).
evidence: Limited Human Studies
summary: A naturally occurring nonapeptide from thymus epithelial cells, active only when bound to zinc, that regulates T-cell development, NK-cell activity, and cytokine production, with possible influence on stress-related hormone regulation. It remains a research compound, not FDA-approved as a drug, though a related thymus-tissue product is approved for congenital athymia.
mechanism: Requires zinc binding for activity; engages JAK/STAT and MAPK pathways in T-cells to raise T-cell marker expression and output of interleukins and interferon-gamma, supporting both cellular and antibody immunity, plus anti-inflammatory effects via reduced NF-κB signaling.
safety: Generally well tolerated in research and clinical use, with occasional fatigue or mild injection-site irritation; not advised for those with thymus disorders or active autoimmune flares without supervision.

name: Tirzepatide
evidence: SURPASS trials: HbA1c reduction 1.24-2.58%, weight loss 5.4-11.7kg. Obesity trials: 19.5-20.9% weight reduction
primaryUse: Type 2 diabetes and chronic weight management
summary: The first dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor co-agonist, approved by the FDA as Mounjaro in 2022 for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound in 2023 for chronic weight management. It has greater affinity for GIP than GLP-1 receptors and produced substantial reductions in blood sugar and body weight in trials.
mechanism: Activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors to stimulate insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and act on brain appetite-regulating centers.
safety: Generally well tolerated; GI side effects are the most common issue.

name: TP508 (Chrysalin)
evidence: Promotes tissue repair/revascularization (diabetic ulcers, fractures). FDA approved for new ARDS clinical trials.
summary: A synthetic 23-amino-acid peptide, Chrysalin, derived from thrombin, discovered in the 1990s to mimic thrombin's tissue-repair effects without its clotting activity. Animal studies show benefits for bone fracture healing, soft tissue repair, and wound closure; human trials for diabetic foot ulcers and fracture healing were promising, but the compound has not reached regulatory approval.
mechanism: Binds the PAR-1 thrombin receptor to trigger angiogenesis, cell migration, and repair pathways, raising VEGF and PDGF, supporting bone-forming cell activity, curbing inflammation via NF-κB modulation, and enhancing bone mineralization and fracture healing through PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling.
safety: Excellent safety record in human trials; no drug-related adverse events reported in diabetic foot ulcer or fracture studies, aside from possible mild injection-site reactions.

name: Tripeptide-29 (Collagen peptide)
approval: Not an approved drug. Widely used in cosmetics and as a GRAS dietary supplement.
evidence: Human clinical trials for both topical and oral use have shown statistically significant improvements in skin wrinkles, elasticity, and hydration.
primaryUse: Skin rejuvenation and collagen production enhancement
summary: Also known as Gly-Pro-Hyp, this synthetic peptide mimics a building block of natural collagen and is used in cosmetics and oral collagen supplements to support skin elasticity, hydration, and matrix strength.
mechanism: Stimulates dermal fibroblasts through TGF-β/SMAD signaling to raise Type I and III collagen genes while regulating matrix-degrading enzymes; also reduces buildup of advanced glycation end products, may inhibit DPP-IV, and drives fibroblast growth and migration via ERK1/2 signaling to support wound healing.
safety: Considered excellent for both topical and oral use.

name: Triptorelin
evidence: FDA-approved GnRH agonist (Trelstar). Standard of care for advanced prostate cancer (androgen deprivation therapy), endometriosis, and central precocious puberty.
primaryUse: Treatment of hormone-dependent cancers and reproductive disorders
summary: A synthetic GnRH agonist decapeptide, first developed in the 1970s, that initially raises then suppresses sex hormones with continued use. An established treatment for prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty, and assisted reproduction, under several brand names.
mechanism: Initially stimulates FSH and LH release, but continuous use downregulates and desensitizes GnRH receptors, suppressing gonadal hormone output to castration levels within one to two weeks after an initial 'flare,' through prolonged receptor binding, calcium mobilization, and protein kinase C activation.
safety: Common effects include hot flashes, reduced libido, and injection-site pain; serious risks include an initial tumor flare, metabolic effects, bone density loss, and rare seizure risk; contraindicated in pregnancy.

name: Trofinetide
evidence: LAVENDER Phase 3: statistically significant improvement on both co-primary endpoints vs placebo
summary: FDA-approved in 2023 as the first drug for Rett syndrome in patients two and older, this synthetic analogue of the IGF-1-derived tripeptide GPE showed statistically significant benefit on co-primary endpoints in the Phase 3 LAVENDER trial, through an unclear mechanism thought to involve neuroprotection.
mechanism: Believed to reduce inflammation, glutamate-driven excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and cell death, though the precise mechanism is unknown.
safety: Most common adverse effects are diarrhea, about 82%, and vomiting, about 29%.

name: Tyroserleutide
evidence: Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials in China. Combination with doxorubicin showed therapeutic synergy
sideEffects: Generally well tolerated based on published trials
summary: A tripeptide (Tyr-Ser-Leu) extracted from pig spleen and developed in China for hepatocellular carcinoma. Phase I trials in advanced HCC were completed, and Phase 2 tested multiple daily doses; research shows it slows tumor growth and metastasis and boosts chemotherapy sensitivity when combined with doxorubicin.
mechanism: Modulates the Ca2+/calmodulin pathway and PI3K activity, and inhibits ICAM-1, MMP-2, and MMP-9 to reduce cancer spread while enhancing chemotherapy effect.
safety: In studies, combination therapy reduced doxorubicin's side effects.

name: Vasopressin
evidence: FDA approved (Vasostrict) for septic shock. Research in acute pain and cardiac arrest.
primaryUse: Blood pressure regulation and water balance maintenance
summary: Also called antidiuretic hormone, this natural hypothalamic peptide regulates fluid balance and blood pressure. Clinically it's a potent vasoconstrictor used for vasodilatory shock, such as septic shock, unresponsive to fluids and other pressor drugs.
mechanism: Acts on kidney V2 receptors via cAMP/PKA signaling to move aquaporin-2 channels to the cell surface, boosting water reabsorption; on blood-vessel V1a receptors it triggers calcium signaling that causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure; centrally, V1b receptors influence social behavior, memory, and stress-hormone regulation.
safety: A potent vasoconstrictor; risks include tissue ischemia, low sodium, and water intoxication; considered safe with ICU monitoring.

name: Vesilute (Glu-Asp-Arg)
evidence: Russian clinical studies for overactive bladder. Limited Western trials.
primaryUse: Bladder and urinary tract health support
summary: A short Russian-researched synthetic peptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) bioregulator meant to normalize bladder function, studied for overactive bladder, chronic cystitis, and prostate-related urinary problems by regulating bladder-wall cell metabolism.
mechanism: Engages membrane receptors to activate COX-2-linked anti-inflammatory pathways and promote epithelial repair via PI3K/Akt signaling, while regulating matrix-degrading enzymes and lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6.
safety: Generally considered safe within its bioregulator class; no significant side effects reported.

name: Vesugen (Lys-Glu-Asp)
evidence: Used in Russia. Limited Western clinical data (2020-2025).
primaryUse: Cardiovascular system support and blood vessel health
summary: A synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) bioregulator studied for vascular health, particularly in older adults, aimed at improving blood flow, reducing atherosclerosis, and supporting blood-vessel wall repair.
mechanism: Acts on vascular endothelial cells via NO/cGMP signaling, boosting nitric oxide synthase activity to aid vasodilation and microcirculation, engaging calcium and PI3K/Akt signaling for endothelial survival and vessel integrity, and modulating VEGF to support controlled vessel repair.
safety: Good short-term safety profile; no significant side effects reported.

name: Vialox (Pentapeptide-3V)
evidence: Limited Human Studies
primaryUse: Reduction of facial wrinkles and expression lines
summary: Marketed sometimes as Syn-Ake, this early-2000s cosmetic peptide mimics Waglerin-1 from temple viper venom to relax facial muscles topically, targeting expression lines. Lab studies show it can reduce muscle-cell contraction, though it remains a cosmetic rather than pharmaceutical ingredient.
mechanism: Reversibly binds the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, blocking acetylcholine from triggering contraction and interfering with SNARE-complex-driven neurotransmitter release, producing a localized, reversible reduction in the micro-contractions that form expression lines.
safety: Good tolerability profile.

name: Vilon (Lys-Glu)
evidence: Synthetic dipeptide bioregulator. Stimulates thymus function and immune response. Investigated for anti-aging and regeneration.
summary: A Russian-developed synthetic dipeptide (Lys-Glu) 'bioregulator' intended to support immune function and slow aging. Studied within Russia but lacking recent research in major international databases; not FDA or EMA approved, and sold online as a supplement or research chemical.
mechanism: Stimulates thymic epithelial cells to boost T-lymphocyte production and maturation, helping counter age-related thymus shrinkage, regulates immune-gene expression, normalizes T-helper/suppressor ratios, and modulates IL-2/IL-4 and JAK/STAT signaling, with possible geroprotective effects via chromatin activation in aging cells.
safety: Described in bioregulator literature as non-toxic with practically no side effects, but this lacks confirmation from rigorous Western clinical trials.

name: VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide)
approval: Not FDA approved as a drug. Has Orphan Drug Designation for pulmonary arterial hypertension.
evidence: Human studies for various conditions including chronic inflammatory response syndrome (CIRS), with ongoing research for diabetes and PCOS.
summary: Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide is a natural 28-amino-acid hormone involved in digestion, immune regulation, and neurological function, acting as a potent vasodilator and anti-inflammatory. Its synthetic form, Aviptadil, has been studied for conditions including respiratory distress and holds Orphan Drug status for pulmonary arterial hypertension, available via compounding pharmacies.
mechanism: Binds VPAC1/VPAC2 receptors to raise cAMP and activate PKA, suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines while boosting anti-inflammatory IL-10; relaxes gut smooth muscle and regulates intestinal secretion and barrier integrity, and shows neuroprotective effects via PI3K/Akt while dampening NF-κB-driven inflammation in immune cells.
safety: Generally considered safe, particularly as a compounded nasal spray.

name: VK2735
evidence: Investigational dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist. Demonstrated significant weight loss in early trials (VENTURE study).
primaryUse: Weight management and metabolic disorder treatment
summary: An early-2020s dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist from Viking Therapeutics, part of a new incretin-based approach targeting both pathways for metabolic disorders. Preclinical and Phase 1 data hint at benefits for weight and metabolic markers, with human studies still ongoing to confirm efficacy and safety.
mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation in the pancreas drives glucose-dependent insulin release and less glucagon, while GIP receptor activation enhances this incretin effect; centrally it activates hypothalamic satiety pathways, and it raises energy expenditure and improves lipid metabolism in fat tissue and the liver.
safety: GI effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are most common, typically mild to moderate and dose-related; no serious drug-related events reported in Phase 1 oral studies; dehydration risk with severe vomiting.

name: Voclosporin
evidence: Positive Phase 3 (AURORA-1) and long-term extension (AURORA-2) trials for lupus nephritis. Included in EULAR and KDIGO clinical guidelines.
primaryUse: Treatment of lupus nephritis in adults
summary: An oral calcineurin inhibitor, FDA-approved in January 2021 as the first oral therapy specifically for active lupus nephritis in adults, used alongside background immunosuppression. Based on the AURORA 1 trial and confirmed by 2024 AURORA 2 extension data showing durable three-year efficacy and safety.
mechanism: Binds cyclophilin A to inhibit calcineurin, blocking NFAT activation and the transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, suppressing T-cell activation and kidney inflammation; may also reduce protein in urine by stabilizing kidney podocytes directly.
safety: Good tolerability profile with monitoring.
boxedWarning: Increased risk of developing malignancies and serious infections.

name: Yorvipath
evidence: PaTHway Phase 3: 78.7% maintained normal calcium levels without conventional treatments vs 4.8% placebo (p<0.0001)
sideEffects: Typical for PTH therapy - hypercalcemia if overdosed
summary: FDA-approved in August 2024 as the first and only treatment for hypoparathyroidism in adults, this once-daily prodrug links PTH(1-34) to a branched PEG carrier via a proprietary linker, slowly releasing the hormone to maintain stable calcium levels without needing active vitamin D or high calcium doses.
mechanism: The TransCon linker technology releases PTH(1-34) gradually over 24 hours, giving continuous hormone exposure that keeps serum calcium in the normal range.
safety: Generally well tolerated.

name: ZP6590 (GIP agonist)
evidence: Animal + In Vitro Studies
primaryUse: Investigational for treating obesity, potentially in combination with GLP-1 agonists.
indication: Investigational - Obesity (in combination with GLP-1 agonists).
sideEffects: Acute pancreatitis (general GLP-1/GIP agonist side effects; specific ZP6590 human data lacking)
summary: An investigational long-acting GIP receptor agonist in preclinical development, with first-in-human trials planned. Preclinical data suggest it enhances weight loss from GLP-1 monotherapy and reduces nausea, positioning it as a potential combination-therapy component for obesity.
mechanism: Selectively binds pancreatic β-cell GIP receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase through Gs-protein coupling to raise cAMP and enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and β-cell function; also affects fat storage and energy balance in adipose tissue and influences nutrient absorption.
safety: No human safety data are available; general GLP-1/GIP agonist concerns include GI side effects, dehydration, kidney function decline, and hypoglycemia risk.
